media.description: On the left, a light blue triangle is outlined in darker blue, with three dashed lines marking off each of its three corners. MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Give the ready-check question about the angles of a triangle something to point at. The three corners of a paper triangle are torn off and laid side by side along a straight line, so the child sees they make a half turn.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first figure of a pair, amber #E69F00 for the second, green #009E73 for a matched pair of parts, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the part being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines, arcs and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a failed match or an impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Flat illustration on a white background, thin dark outlines, flat fills. Left half: one paper triangle in teal, each of its three corners marked with a small dashed tear line. Right half: the same three corners torn off and laid tip to tip along one straight grey line, with a thin green arc sweeping across all three. There is no text in the frame.

Exact mathematical structure:
- The left half shows one triangle with a small dashed tear line across each of its three corners.
- The right half shows exactly three torn corners, laid tip to tip with their points touching on one straight grey line and no gaps or overlaps.
- A thin green arc sweeps across all three corners together, ending on the straight line at both ends.
- No numbers, no degree sign and no words anywhere in the frame.

Visible text:
- none; the frame carries no text at all

Critical rejection conditions:
- a number, degree sign or caption that gives the total of the three angles
- the three corners on the right left with gaps between them or not lying on one straight line
- a fourth corner or a piece of the triangle that is not a corner
- any orange or muted red, because nothing here fails
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle
- tick marks that do not match the equal sides and angles stated, or a pair of figures that is not congruent when the picture says it is

Student takeaway: The three corners of a triangle fit together along a straight line.

video_script.anchor: Are two numbers enough to paint the same symbol?
video_script.design: One idea: two lengths leave the angle between them free, so three numbers are needed. It assumes the child can measure a length with a ruler and an opening with a protractor. The wrong idea is some students's: every painter obeyed the notebook so every symbol is the same. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap.
source: Painting the signboard twice: what to measure
Would another measurement help? Draw it with the angle
never_show: a verdict that all four symbols are the same
the answer to the your-turn question: the angle where the two sticks meet
video_script.wrong_move: some students thinks that because every painter obeyed the notebook, every symbol must be identical; the first symbol then slides along the row and fails to land on three of the four.
maths_rules: The first symbol has an arm AB of 4 cm and an arm BC of 8 cm meeting at B, with the angle at B equal to 80 degrees.
Each of the four painters draws arms of exactly 4 cm and 8 cm, so the four amber symbols differ from one another only in the elbow.

One amber symbol has its elbow at 80 degrees, so it matches the first symbol exactly and the first symbol lands on it. The other three are drawn with visibly different elbows (one narrower, one wider and flatter, one bent the other way) and the first symbol fails to land on each of them. That is why it fails on three of the four. No elbow angle is written on screen before the reveal.
some students's claim, that all four signs must be the same, fails because the first symbol lands on only one of the four.
After the angle is added, all four painters redraw with AB = 4 cm, BC = 8 cm and angle at B = 80 degrees, so all four redrawn symbols are identical and the first symbol lands on each one.
your turn: two sticks of 30 cm and 50 cm joined at one end; the missing number is the angle between them, never shown.

maths_rules: The first pair is two curvy blob shapes of exactly the same shape and size, the left one teal and the right one amber.
The tracing of the left blob is an exact copy of its outline, so when it is dropped on the right blob every edge coincides and the pair turns green.
The second pair is two round discs, each with a wedge cut out like a mouth, of exactly the same shape and size, so the tracing lands exactly on them too.
Size means every length and every angle together, not one total such as the area.
Sliding the tracing does not change it, so the test is allowed.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question, before the tracing is dropped): Before we drop it, guess. Will the tracing land exactly, or will something stick out? Answer: it will land exactly. Also accept: land, it will fit, yes, exactly, same. If stuck: Just guess. A guess costs nothing here. If wrong (something will stick out): Good instinct to doubt, doubting is the right habit. Watch what the tracing does. Stop 2 (after the test on the second pair): Here is the word again. Say it back: what does congruent mean? Answer: one lands exactly on the other. Also accept: same shape and size, they fit on top of each other, exact copy, they match exactly, you can put one on the other. If stuck: Describe what the tracing paper just did. If wrong (they look the same): Close, but look is the word we are trying to get rid of. What did we do to be sure? Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two flags are cut from one pattern, with sides of ten and eleven centimetres. Are the two flags congruent? Answer: no, the tracing of the small flag leaves a gap all round the bigger one, because size means every length. Also accept: no, not the same size, the tracing will not land, the big one sticks out. If stuck: What would the tracing of the small flag do when you drop it on the big one? Does it cover it? If wrong (yes, same shape): Same shape is only half of it. What does size mean here, and does the tracing cover the big flag? Watch for the child who says size means area: it means every length and every angle, not one total. This video is the first that uses the word congruent. The disc pair is congruent on purpose, so that the child does not learn that a pair which looks the same is a trick.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the hook): One bracket sits flat and one balances on a corner. Same shape or different shapes? If the child needs it rephrased: forget which way up they are, do the corners match? Answer: same. Also accept: same, the same, congruent, yes same, they are twins. If stuck: Forget which way up they are. Trace one in the air with your finger and compare the corners. If wrong (different): You are in enormous company, this one catches almost everybody, and it stays caught for years if nobody shows you. Watch the tracing paper turn. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): This pair are mirror images. Can I get from one to the other by turning alone? Answer: no, you have to flip it. Also accept: no, you have to flip it, no flip, need to turn it over. If stuck: Try it with your two hands. Can you spin your left hand into your right? If wrong (yes): Give it a try in your head, spin it a quarter, a half, all the way round. The bump stays on the wrong side. There is a second move we need. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A flag has a copy that is turned a hundred and fifty degrees and also mirrored. Which two moves does the tracing need to land? Answer: a turn and a flip, in either order. Also accept: turn and flip, flip and turn, rotate and flip, turn it and turn it over. If stuck: Is the copy a mirror image? Which move changes a figure into its mirror image? If wrong (turn only): Spin it as far as you like. Does the flag ever become its own mirror image by turning? Watch for M2: a child who calls a turned figure different is never corrected with words. Hand over the tracing overlay and let the figure land. Watch for M10: a child who says twins must sit in the same place is shown the chair, four positions, one chair. The slide is defined here once, for the later videos that use the word.

media.title: Twin Checker
media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'What Makes Two Things Twins', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
The student opens a stage split by a thin vertical line. On the left, a fixed amber outline of one figure is the target. On the right, a translucent grey sheet of tracing paper carries a teal outline of a second figure, and the whole sheet can be dragged. A move bar has three large buttons: slide (on by default), turn (a ring handle appears with the angle in degrees) and flip (one tap mirrors the sheet). A verdict strip along the bottom has three states only: not touching, overlapping but not landed, and landed. The challenge card sits at the bottom left, with a reset arrow at the top left.

On each card the student first predicts whether the tracing will land exactly or something will stick out. Then the student drags the sheet over the target, turns it with the ring, flips it, and watches the strip. With no gap and no overhang it says landed: 'Landed. Not a gap anywhere.' A near miss says 'Close. Look at the gap.' Pressing twins before the sheet has landed gets 'Show me. Make it land first,' so a verdict is earned by landing, not by looking. The student presses not twins only when no moving can work; on a pair that can land the tool says 'Not so fast. Try flipping it over.'

The seven cards climb in steps. Card 1 is two identical arrows, one slid to the right, so sliding alone lands it. Card 2 is a pair of L-shaped brackets, the second turned 100 degrees. Card 3 is two semicircle shapes that are mirror images, which only a flip lands. Card 4 is a flag turned 150 degrees and flipped, so both moves are needed. Card 5 shows the two signboard symbols with arms of 4 and 8 and angles of 80 and 55 degrees: the arms match but the elbow does not, so it never lands and the student presses not twins. Card 6 shows squares of side 5 and 6 centimetres; the student presses not twins and picks the reason, that one is bigger and no move changes size. Card 7 shows a target and three candidates, a turned copy, a flipped copy and a slightly wider copy, and the student finds the two that land.

Hints ask what the student did to be sure, since looking is a guess and the tracing is the test; then which of slide, turn and flip are still untried; then whether any edge still sticks out however the sheet is moved. Afterwards a tray of twelve loose figures opens, arrows, brackets, leaves and blobs in two sizes each. Nothing is asked: the student drags any two onto the stage and tests them while a quiet counter reads pairs tested. Through doing, the student learns that congruent means one lands exactly on the other, that sliding, turning and flipping never change a length or an angle, and that a pair of different sizes can never land.

A symbol painted on one signboard must be painted exactly the same on a second board across town. What can the painter carry across, and are the two arm lengths, four centimetres and eight centimetres, enough?
1. Tracing paper would have to be as tall as the board, so the painter carries numbers instead.
2. Name the corners A, B and C, with B at the elbow, and measure arm AB and arm BC.
3. Four painters follow AB = 4 cm and BC = 8 cm and paint four different symbols.
4. Three of the four do not land on the original, so the two lengths are not enough.
Answer: No. The two lengths leave the opening of the elbow free, so different symbols fit the same notebook.

content.text:
Would any other measurement help? Draw the symbol with AB = 4 cm, BC = 8 cm and the angle at B equal to 80 degrees.
1. Measure the angle at the elbow, between the two arms: it is 80 degrees.
2. Write it as a third line in the notebook: AB = 4 cm, BC = 8 cm, angle at B = 80 degrees.
3. Draw an arm of 4 cm, then 80 degrees at its end, then an arm of 8 cm.
4. Every painter now draws the same symbol: only one is possible.
Answer: Yes. The angle between the two arms, 80 degrees, together with the two lengths fixes the symbol: three measurements are enough.

content.text:
Two figures are congruent when one lands exactly on the other. The test is one you can do with your hands: trace one figure, pick the tracing up, carry it across and drop it on the other.
It fits or it does not. If every edge of the tracing coincides with the second figure, with no gap and no overhang, the two figures are congruent.
Congruent means the same shape and the same size. Size here means everything: every length and every angle, not only how much space the figure covers.
A second pair, two round discs with a wedge cut out, looks identical at a glance. Do not trust your eyes. Test it. This pair lands exactly too, so it is congruent. Looking is a good guess. Landing is proof.

content.text:
A figure does not stop being itself when it is moved. There are three moves. Slide moves it without turning it. Turn spins it where it is. Flip turns it over, like turning over a sheet.
A bracket sits flat. A second bracket stands on a corner, as if it might fall over. It looks different, yet the tracing of the first, turned through 100 degrees, lands on the second with no gap anywhere.
Turning is allowed. A twin can be lying at any angle.
Now take two figures that are mirror images of each other. Turning will never land one on the other, however long you spin. Pick the tracing up and turn it over, like a sheet, and it lands. Flipping is allowed too.
Turning and flipping are different moves. A left glove never becomes a right glove by spinning it. Where a figure sits on the paper does not matter either: one chair can stand upright, lie on its back, hang upside down or be seen from the other side, and it is still one chair.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the circle prediction, in the hook): Before I write anything, how many numbers do you think a circle needs? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: any number, or I do not know. If the child says one, say: hold that thought, and watch me prove you right. If stuck: Just throw a number out. One? Two? Ten? If wrong: none, a prediction cannot be wrong; repeat the child's number back warmly and say let us see. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip, the rectangle): How many numbers does the rectangle really need? Answer: two, the length and the breadth. Also accept: 2, two, length and breadth, two numbers, length and width. If stuck: Which measurements could you change and still have a rectangle? If wrong (four, one for each side): Good thinking, four sides, four numbers. But look at the opposite sides. Do you really need to measure both of them? If wrong (three): Which three? Say them out loud, I think you will find one of them is already decided for you. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A photo frame is a rectangle, twenty centimetres long and fifteen centimetres wide. Which numbers does the shop need to copy it? Answer: the length and the breadth, two numbers, and no angle. Also accept: length and width, twenty and fifteen, two numbers. If stuck: Think of the rectangle with six and four. What did we write in the notebook? If wrong (the four sides, or an angle): The opposite sides are equal and every corner is a right angle already. Which numbers are left? The sentence the child should be able to say afterwards: for each kind of shape there is a shortest list of measurements, and it is usually shorter than I expect.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Give the question what do you need to tell the painter something to point at. A signpost with three boards of different lengths stands beside an identical post with blank boards, so the child must say what the painter has to be told.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first figure of a pair, amber #E69F00 for the second, green #009E73 for a matched pair of parts, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the part being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines, arcs and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a failed match or an impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Flat illustration on a white background, thin dark outlines, flat fills. Two wooden signposts side by side at a dusty village crossing. The left post has three painted arrow-boards nailed to it, pointing three different ways. The right post is identical but its three boards are blank. One line of text runs across the bottom of the frame.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly 2 signposts are drawn, the same height and the same wood.
- The left post carries 3 arrow-boards pointing three different ways, and the three boards are clearly different lengths.
- The right post carries 3 blank boards in the same places as the left post's boards, with no arrowheads and no paint on them.
- No number, length, angle or measurement appears anywhere in the frame.

Visible text:
- Same post, same boards: what do you need to tell the painter?

Critical rejection conditions:
- any length, angle or number drawn or written on a board
- the three boards drawn the same length, because the lengths must be clearly different
- a label, caption or arrow that says what the painter must measure
- any source reference or logo of any kind
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle
- tick marks that do not match the equal sides and angles stated, or a pair of figures that is not congruent when the picture says it is

Student takeaway: Before copying a figure, ask what could still change: each board's length and the angles between the boards.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): How would you check whether two figures like this one, three roads from one crossing, are congruent? What would you measure? Answer: the three road lengths and the angles between the roads. Also accept: measure each road, lengths and angles, the sides and the angles, lay a tracing over it, how long each road is and how they are spread. If stuck: Hold three pencils meeting at a point on your desk. Which parts of the picture could you put a tape or a protractor against? If wrong (only lengths): A length is part of it. What could still change about how the roads are spread? Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): I have written all three lengths down. Is the figure pinned, or can it still move? Answer: it can still move. Also accept: still move, it can move, not pinned, no it can swing, the arms can turn. If stuck: Hold three pencils meeting at a point on your desk. Keep them the same length. Can you still change the picture? If wrong (pinned): Have a look at what happens next. I am keeping every length exactly the same and the picture still changes. Stop 3 (after the two angles): I know two of the three angles round the crossing. Do I need to measure the third? Answer: no. Also accept: no, you can work it out, it is the full turn minus the other two, it is whatever is left. If stuck: How many degrees is it all the way round a point? If wrong (yes): You could measure it, and nothing is wrong with that. But watch, it is already decided. Watch for M1: a child who says the lengths are enough is told, let us swing the roads and see. The fix is always the swing, never a scolding. The video measures the first pair on screen as a worked model and then stops. The other two pairs are left for the child to measure, and no verdict is given for them. The full turn is three hundred and sixty degrees. Five measurements: three lengths and two angles.

media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'What Would You Measure?', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
The student sits at a painter's desk. On the left is the original figure in teal, with a small grey chip beside each measurable part, such as side AB, angle B or radius. On the right is a lined notebook headed by a running count, Numbers written. One big button, send it, sits at the bottom centre. A picker of seven shape icons chooses the figure, and a record strip at the top right keeps the smallest list found so far for each shape.

The student taps a chip, which shows its value and writes it as a line in the notebook; tapping it again rubs the line out. Before sending, the student may press forced or not forced to record a guess about whether four painters across town will draw the same figure. The tool never requires the guess, but it notes when it was right. Send it turns the right half into a copy shop where four painters each draw a figure that obeys every line. If something is still free, the four drawings differ, sit side by side in amber and carry warning markers: 'Four painters, four answers. Something is still free to move.' If the list forces the figure, the four stack into one outlined in green with the word FORCED. A longer list than needed gets 'That works, but could you take one away?' and a shorter one than before gets 'New record.' Try a shorter list clears the notebook on the same shape.

Card 1 is a circle: one number, the radius. Card 2 is a 6 by 4 rectangle: length and breadth, since the corners are right angles already. Card 3 is the signboard symbol with arms of 4 and 8: two numbers send back four different symbols, and the student finds the third, the angle between the arms. Card 4 is a square of side 5, which needs one number. Card 5 is three roads from a crossing: three lengths and two angles make five numbers, because the third angle is what is left of the full turn. Card 6 asks the student to force a triangle using angles only. However many angles are written, the four painters draw four sizes, so the student presses impossible and picks the reason: angles fix the shape but not the size. Card 7 lets the student pick any shape.

Hints ask which measurements could change while the shape stays the same kind, since those must go on the list; then which could not change, since those need no place; then what happens to the four drawings when one line is taken out. Free play unlocks every shape, plus a parallelogram, a regular hexagon and a five-pointed star, and a pad for drawing a closed figure of up to six corners. Through doing, the student learns that a list is long enough exactly when nobody can draw a second, different figure that obeys it, and that angles alone never fix a size.

content.publication_text: A circle has to be described to someone across town, using numbers only. How many numbers do you think it needs?

content.text:
The question can be turned around. Instead of asking are these two congruent, ask what you would need to know to copy the shape exactly. For every kind of shape there is a shortest list of measurements, and when the list matches, the shapes are twins.
A circle needs one number, the radius. Anyone who sets a compass to that radius draws the very same circle, and there is no second answer.
A rectangle needs two numbers, the length and the breadth. The corners are all right angles already, so nobody has to be told. The signboard symbol needs three: the two arms and the angle between them.
To check two shapes of one kind, compare the numbers on their list. Two circles are congruent when their radii are equal. Two rectangles are congruent when the lengths match and the breadths match. The list is usually much shorter than you expect.

content.text:
If two symbols have the same arm lengths, can we say they are congruent?

2. Matching arms leave the elbow free to open any amount, so the angle between the arms still has to be compared.
3. Two arm lengths alone cannot settle it. The list for this symbol has three numbers: both arms and the angle between them.
Answer: No. The same arm lengths are not enough, because the angle between the arms can still be different.

video_script.anchor: Both arms match: are these two symbols congruent?
video_script.design: One idea: matching arms are not enough, so decide with all the measurements, and then sort pairs by size and shape. It assumes the child has seen the four painters and the tracing test. The wrong idea is some students's: he stops at the two arms. The anchor question stays up from the hook to the break; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap. Meera and Rabia do not appear.

an exact elbow angle stated as certain: the readings are about one hundred and three and about eighty-three
video_script.wrong_move: some students stops measuring after the two arms match and says congruent; the protractor then reads about one hundred and three degrees on one elbow and about eighty-three on the other, so the tracing of one cannot land on the other.
maths_rules: Two V-shaped symbols, one teal and one amber, are drawn side by side; the short arms are equal in length and the long arms are equal in length.

The elbow of the teal symbol reads about 103 degrees and the elbow of the amber symbol reads about 83 degrees, measured off the picture, so the readings are shown as about and the two figures are not congruent.
some students says congruent after matching only the two arms; the protractor readings show the elbows differ, so his idea is struck.

Four pairs are shown in a grid: teardrops, clouds, starbursts and leaf-pairs. The teardrops land after a flip and the leaf-pairs land after a turn. In the clouds and in the starbursts one figure is plainly bigger than the other, so neither pair lands.
Two pairs out of four are congruent: the teardrops and the leaf-pairs.
A circle is checked by one number, the radius: two circles are congruent exactly when the radii are equal.
A rectangle is checked by two numbers, the length and the breadth: a rectangle of 6 by 4 and a rectangle of 4 by 6 are congruent, because one is the other turned.
The two circles carry a radius line each and no number before the child answers.
video_script.payoff_line: Matching arms are not enough

final_answer.value: Not congruent: the arms match but the elbows differ (about 103 degrees against about 83 degrees)
final_answer.spoken: not congruent, because the arms match but the elbows are clearly different

video_script.substitution: Matching arms leave the elbow free, so compare the angle too; for a circle compare the radii, and for a rectangle compare the length and the breadth.
video_script.wrong_answer: both arms match, so they are congruent

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): Both arms match on these two symbols. Are they congruent? Answer: no. Also accept: no, not sure yet, need the angle, we do not know yet, check the angle. If stuck: Think back to the four painters. If wrong (yes): This is the trap from Topic 1 wearing a new hat. Two arms are never enough, so watch the protractor. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): What could still be different between these two symbols? Answer: the angle at the elbow. Also accept: the angle, the elbow, how wide it opens, the bend. If stuck: Put two fingers in a V and keep both fingers the same length. What can you still change? If wrong (the length): The lengths already match. What else about the V could still differ? Stop 3 (after the four pairs): What would you compare to check that two circles are congruent? Answer: compare the radii. Also accept: see if the radius is the same, measure both radii, compare the diameters, check they are the same size, same radius. If stuck: Think about what you would measure on a circle. Now say what you would compare. If wrong (trace them): That works, and it is a fine answer, but the point here is that you do not have to. One number does it. Watch for M1: the clouds and the starbursts are the same shape in different sizes. A child who circles them has judged by outline alone. The fix is always the overlay, never a scolding. Honesty note: the two elbow readings, about one hundred and three and about eighty-three degrees, are measured off the picture, so the video says about and gives the reasoning. The rectangle of six by four and the one of four by six are congruent, because one is the other turned.

maths_rules: The wooden frame has sides of 40 cm, 60 cm and 80 cm; the smaller triangle on the paper has sides of 4 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm, which is the frame shrunk to a tenth so that a child can try it on a paper.
Put A at (0, 0) and B at (6, 0), so AB = 6 cm. The circle round A has radius 4 and the circle round B has radius 8.

The circles cross at E = (-1, 3.873) above the line and F = (-1, -3.873) below it. Check: AE = sqrt(1 + 15) = 4 and BE = sqrt(49 + 15) = 8, and the same for F. Both crossing points lie 1 cm to the left of A, beyond it along the line BA extended.

E and F are mirror images in the line AB, so folding the paper along AB puts E exactly on F, and the two triangles coincide.
some students's claim fails because a flip is allowed: triangle ABF is triangle ABE turned over, so there was only ever one triangle.

media.teaching_notes: Folded hook: this video opens with the Flow hook Put the Protractor Down. Its one prediction question is the first stop; it is a prediction and cannot be wrong. Store the side the child took and name it again after the fold: you said Rabia, so let us see. Stop 1 (the end of the opening scene, before any test): Meera says three sides are enough. Rabia wants the angles too. Who do you think is right? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: Meera, Rabia, both, I do not know, it depends. If stuck: There is no way to know yet. Just pick the one that feels right. If wrong: none, a hook question cannot be wrong; say noted, I will hold you to that in about three minutes. Stop 2 (the circles have just crossed): How many places do the two circles cross at? Answer: two. Also accept: 2, two, twice, two points, E and F. If stuck: Count the dots where the two dashed circles meet. If wrong (one): Look at the bottom of the picture as well, there is a second meeting below the line. Stop 3 (after Chintu's slip): Chintu says two crossings means two different triangles, so Meera is wrong. Do you agree with Chintu? Answer: no. Also accept: no, they are the same, it is a flip, they are twins, no it is flipped over. If stuck: Look hard at the two triangles. Is the bottom one really a different shape, or the same one upside down? If wrong (yes, Chintu is right): That is exactly where I would be too. Keep watching, the paper is about to fold, and I think it will change your mind. Never correct this with words; the fold does the correcting. Stop 4 (the fold): Fold along the line A B. Where does E land? Answer: on F. Also accept: on F, F, exactly on F, on top of F. If stuck: Watch the fold again. Follow E with your eye. If wrong: Keep your eye only on the point E and run it once more. Stop 5 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two triangles each have sides of nine, twelve and fifteen centimetres. Are the two triangles congruent? Answer: yes, they are congruent, because three sides leave the triangle nowhere to move, and no angles are needed. Also accept: yes, same three sides, side side side, yes without measuring the angles. If stuck: Where could the third corner go, if two circles fix it? If wrong (I need the angles): You can measure them and you will be right, but you would be doing work that the three sides have already done. Watch for M2: a child who says triangle A B E and triangle A B F are different has not accepted the flip; go back to the tracing paper before going on. Watch for M7: a child who wants to measure the angles after side side side has settled it is told warmly that they may, and that the work is already done.

Three teal sticks lie loose on a bench in front of the student, each with a round hinge at both ends and its length printed along it. Dragging one end near another snaps them into a hinge, and dragging a joint swings the sticks about it. Three sliders on the left set the lengths from 1 to 12 centimetres. On the right, a gallery keeps every closed triangle built on the card as a small thumbnail, under a line that reads Different triangles found: 1. A flip button, a turn ring and a wobble button along the bottom act on whatever is on the bench.

Before building, the student predicts whether the same three sticks can make two triangles that are not twins. The student sets 4, 6 and 8, hinges the ends and swings the joints until the triangle closes: 'Closed. Nothing can move now.' Add to gallery saves it. Then the student tries to build a different one, by swinging the joints another way, or flipping and turning what is on the bench, and adds it again. A congruent build is stacked on the first thumbnail with a green edge and counted as one: 'Same triangle. It's just lying differently.' A genuinely different build would sit apart, but with three fixed lengths it never does. Wobble on the closed triangle gives 'It won't budge,' while two sticks hinged but not closed flop about.

Card 4 builds Meera's 40, 60 and 80 centimetre frame as a model at a tenth of the size, 4, 6 and 8, and meets the same triangle again. Card 5 builds 5, 5 and 8 and flips it: the flip lands on itself, because this triangle has a fold line of its own. Card 6 asks for a triangle from 2, 3 and 9. The sticks will not meet, so the student presses impossible and picks the reason: two and three together are shorter than nine. Card 7 asks for two triangles from 6, 7 and 10 that are not twins. Every attempt lands on the first, so the student presses impossible with the reason that three sides fix everything and any build is the first one turned or flipped.

Hints ask what the wobble does to the shape; then what the two shorter sticks add up to compared with the longest; then whether the new build, flipped or turned, covers the thumbnail already in the gallery. In free play the sliders reach 20 centimetres and a fourth stick appears, which wobbles. Through doing, the student learns that three fixed lengths leave a closed triangle no freedom, that a triangle closes only when two sides together are longer than the third, and that this is why a three-sided frame holds its shape.

content.text:
Meera and Rabia have a job. A large wooden triangular frame leans against the corridor wall, and they must make an exact cardboard copy of it. The frame is taller than both girls.
Tracing paper is no use, because the sheet covers only a small part of the frame. So they measure. The sides come to forty centimetres, sixty centimetres and eighty centimetres.
Rabia reaches for her protractor to measure the corners next. Meera stops her. She says they do not need the angles, because three sides are enough.
Nobody knows yet who is right, and that is the question. Take a side now. The test comes in the next part, and your answer will be named then.
To test it by drawing, shrink the frame. Forty, sixty and eighty centimetres become four, six and eight centimetres, and the shape is the same.

content.text:
Follow Rabia's way of drawing the triangle. Draw the base AB, six centimetres long. The corner E must be four centimetres from A, so it sits somewhere on a circle of radius four centimetres around A.
The corner must also be eight centimetres from B, so it sits on a circle of radius eight centimetres around B. The corner is where the two circles cross.
The circles cross in two places, E above the line AB and F below it. That gives two triangles, ABE and ABF, and it looks as if three sides left a choice.
Look at where E and F sit. They are mirror images across the line AB. Fold the paper along AB and E lands exactly on F, so the two triangles land on each other.
A flip is allowed, so ABE and ABF are twins. There was only ever one triangle, drawn the right way up and then flipped over.
So if two triangles have the same three sides, they are congruent. This is called the SSS condition: side, side, side.

Is it enough to know the three sides, four centimetres, six centimetres and eight centimetres? Can you draw such a triangle?
1. Draw the base AB of 6 cm.
2. The corner must be 4 cm from A, so it lies on a circle of radius 4 cm around A.

5. Join E to A and to B. The triangle ABE has sides 6 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, so such a triangle can be drawn.
Answer: Yes. A triangle with sides 4 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm can be drawn. The two circles cross at the corner, and the angles come out as about 104.5 degrees at A, 29 degrees at B and 46.6 degrees at E.

content.text:
The two circles cross at E and F. Examine whether triangle ABE and triangle ABF are congruent. You may trace and compare, cut out and place one on the other, or notice that AB is a fold line.
1. Both triangles have the base AB = 6 cm, and AE = AF = 4 cm and BE = BF = 8 cm, because E and F are both crossing points of the same two circles.
2. E and F are mirror images across the line AB: they sit the same distance above and below it.
3. Fold the paper along AB and E lands exactly on F, so triangle ABE lands exactly on triangle ABF.
4. A flip is allowed, so the two triangles are congruent, with A on A, B on B and E on F.
5. So all triangles with the same three side lengths are congruent: this is the SSS condition.
Answer: Yes, triangle ABE is congruent to triangle ABF, because one is the other flipped over the line AB. If two triangles have the same three sides, they are congruent (SSS).

content.text:
If two triangles have the same side lengths, then they are congruent. This is called the SSS condition for congruence. Do the sides five, eight, eleven and eleven, five, eight make twins? Do six, six, nine and six, nine, nine?
1. Match five with five, eight with eight and eleven with eleven. All three sides have a partner, so the first pair are twins.
2. In six, six, nine and six, nine, nine, one six pairs with one six and the nine pairs with one nine.
3. The second six has no partner and the second nine has no partner, so only two of the three sides match.
4. The SSS condition needs all three sides to match, so the second pair are not twins.
Answer: Five, eight, eleven and eleven, five, eight are twins. Six, six, nine and six, nine, nine are not twins.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): To decide which corner lands on which, do you look at the corners first, or at the sides? Answer: the sides. Also accept: sides, the sides, look at the sides, I am not sure, the corners. If stuck: Think about turning one triangle round on the paper. Does a corner stay at the top? If wrong (the corners): Many people start there, and it is exactly the trap. Keep watching, the tilt of the paper is about to fool Chintu. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): Which side of the right-hand triangle must land on the shortest side of the left one? Answer: the shortest one. Also accept: the shortest, the shortest side, the small one, the one with the single bar. If stuck: If a long side landed on a short side, what would stick out? If wrong (the longest): Try it in your head, put the long one on the short one. One of them hangs over the end. Stop 3 (after the corners are matched and the angles are lit): Did anybody measure angle eigh or angle X? Answer: no. Also accept: no, nobody, no it is free, it just lands there. If stuck: Did a protractor appear anywhere in that animation? If wrong (yes): Run it back, there was never a protractor on screen. That is the point of this video. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): Triangle H I J has its shortest side H I and its longest side I J. Its twin Q R S has its shortest side Q R and its longest side R S. Which corner of Q R S lands on J? Answer: S. Also accept: S, corner S, it lands on S. If stuck: Which side of the twin lands on side I J, and which end of it is left after I has been placed? If wrong (R): R is already used by I. Put the shortest sides together first, then the longest, and see which corner is left. media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): A second statement uses the same six letters with the left side in a new order, triangle ACB is congruent to triangle XYZ. Does it record the same match? If the child needs it rephrased: does it say the same thing about which corner lands on which? Answer: no, it records a different match. Also accept: no, not the same, different, it is wrong, it changes the matching, the order matters. If stuck: Read the statement out loud one letter from each side at a time. Which letter goes with C? If wrong (yes, any order works): That is what most people say, and it is why this video exists. Keep watching, we will do exactly what the statement says and see where the triangle lands. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): Chintu wrote triangle ACB is congruent to triangle XYZ. Following that literally, which corner does C land on? Answer: Y. Also accept: Y, on Y, the second one. If stuck: C is the second letter on the left. Point at the second letter on the right. If wrong (Z): Count the positions, not the alphabet. C is sitting in the second slot. Stop 3 (the fix): He now wants to keep triangle ACB on the left. What must he write on the right? Answer: triangle XZY. Also accept: XZY, X Z Y, swap Y and Z, swap the second and third letters. If stuck: He swapped the second and third letters on the left. Do the same on the right. If wrong (XYZ): That is the one that just failed. He changed the left side, so the right side has to change to match. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): Triangle GHJ is congruent to triangle STU. Chintu rewrites the left side as JGH. What must he write on the right? Answer: triangle UST, because J was third so U goes first, G was first so S goes second, H was second so T goes third. Also accept: UST, U S T, move the third letter to the front, shuffle the right side the same way. If stuck: Say which slot each left letter used to be in. J was third, so which letter on the right was third? If wrong (STU): That is the original order. The left side changed, so the right side must change in the same way. Watch for M5: a child who writes a wrong order is never told the order is wrong. They are told to read it out as an instruction and say where C lands. The new term here is congruence statement. The fourth statement about this pair, triangle ABC with triangle XZY, fails the same way and is left for the picture of four statements.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): How many triangles are in this picture? Answer: two. Also accept: 2, two, two triangles. If stuck: Trace the line from corner to corner with your finger. What is above it? What is below it? If wrong (one): There is one above the line and one below it. Run your finger round each. Stop 2 (after the two pairs from the rectangle): Two sides are matched from the rectangle. Where does the third match come from? Answer: it is the same side in both triangles. Also accept: it is shared, it is in both, it is the same line, B D is in both, free side, it is equal to itself. If stuck: Look at the two separated triangles. Is there a side that was the same actual line before we pulled them apart? If wrong (you measure it): You could. But look, it is the same line, drawn once, sitting in both triangles. It cannot help being equal to itself. Stop 3 (after Chintu's slip): Chintu writes triangle A B D is congruent to triangle C B D. Which side does that lay side A B onto? Answer: C B. Also accept: C B, B C, the short one, the side from C to B. If stuck: A is in the first place and B is in the second. Read off the first and second letters of the other name. If wrong: Read the two statements in step: A with C, B with B. So A B lands on C, and then on which letter? Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): A rectangle P Q R S is cut corner to corner. Which side do triangle P Q R and triangle R S P share? Answer: the side P R. Also accept: P R, R P, the line from P to R, the cut. If stuck: Pull the two triangles apart in your mind. Which side was one line before the pull? If wrong (a side of the rectangle): That side belongs to only one of the triangles. Look for the letters that appear in both names. Watch for M6: the habit to install is, pull the two triangles apart before counting anything. The talk image of one wall and two rooms comes before this video and asks the shared-line question with no triangle in sight.

media.title: Name the Twins
media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'Writing the Match Down', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
Two congruent triangles lie at different tilts on the stage, the left one teal and the right one amber, each with its corners labelled. Tick marks show which sides are equal, but the labels are not arranged helpfully. Below them is a statement bar with six empty slots: a triangle sign, three slots, the congruent sign, a triangle sign and three more slots. Two trays hold draggable letter tiles, the three letters of each triangle. A big OBEY IT button sits at the bottom with CLEAR, SHOW TICKS or HIDE TICKS, and ROTATE amber. A counter reads correct ways found, for example 2 of 6, and never nags.

The student drags letters into the slots, predicts whether the statement will land or leave a corner hanging, and presses OBEY IT. The teal triangle flies onto the amber one exactly as written, slot 1 onto slot 4, slot 2 onto slot 5, slot 3 onto slot 6, right or wrong. A correct statement lands exactly, 'It landed. That statement is a correct one,' and is saved in the counter. A wrong one lands crooked, a long side on a short side, with the overhanging corner in the failure colour, and stays until the student changes the statement: 'Look where it put the corners. Follow your own letters.' So a wrong statement is an instruction followed to the letter. ROTATE amber spins the amber triangle, so the student can check that a correct answer does not depend on how it lies.

Card 1 asks for triangle ABC and triangle XYZ to land. Card 2 asks for a second correct way, such as ACB with XZY. Card 3 asks for all six. Card 4 gives triangle HEN and triangle BIG and asks for the other five: HNE with BGI, EHN with IBG, ENH with IGB, NHE with GBI and NEH with GIB. Card 5 is the rectangle cut along BD, triangle ABD and triangle CDB. In card 6 Chintu wrote triangle ABD and triangle CBD. The student presses OBEY IT, watches it land crooked, and names the fault from three choices; the true one is that it puts a long side on a short side. In card 7 the student is asked for a correct statement with A matched to Y in a pair where A has to go to X. No order works, so the student presses impossible and gives the reason that A's two sides are a long and a medium one while Y's are a medium and a short one.

Hints ask the student to read the letters one by one, first on first, second on second, third on third; then to look at the sides before the corners, since the shortest sides must land on each other; then, on the rectangle pair, to pull the triangles apart and mark the shared side first. In free play a shuffle button brings new pairs with the ticks hidden. Through doing, the student learns that a congruence statement is an instruction, that six statements say the same thing, and that shuffling only one name says something else.

content.text: Which side of one triangle must land on which side of the other, and what does that tell you about the corners? Say what you think before you test it: can you decide the matching by looking at the corners, or do you need the sides? Draw a triangle with three different sides on one sheet. content.text:
The two triangles ABC and XYZ are congruent and lie at different tilts. Which corners should be placed on each other so that the equal sides overlap? Are there other ways of overlapping them so that they fit exactly?
1. Find the shortest side of each triangle, the one with a single bar. These two sides must land on each other.
2. Their end corners must land on each other too. Take the next side of each, with two bars, and then the last side, with three bars, and check the same way.
3. The corners that land on each other are A on X, B on Y and C on Z.
4. The three sides of each triangle are all different, so every side has only one partner. Any other pairing puts a long side on a short one and leaves an end sticking out.
5. Because A sits on X, B on Y and C on Z, angle A equals angle X, angle B equals angle Y and angle C equals angle Z. Nobody had to measure them.
Answer: Place A over X, B over Y and C over Z. There is no other way, because the three sides are all different. The angles are equal as a result: angle A = angle X, angle B = angle Y, angle C = angle Z.

content.text:
Once you know which corner lands on which, you write it down. Many children treat this as a spelling rule. It is not. You are not naming the triangles. You are sending a message in six letters that says how to lay one triangle on the other.
Read ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ as an instruction. First letter with first letter: put A on X. Second letter with second letter: put B on Y. Third letter with third letter: put C on Z.
Now follow Chintu's statement, ΔACB ≅ ΔXYZ, exactly as it is written. A goes on X, but C is the second letter, so it goes on Y. A long side lands on a short side and a corner hangs over the end. The message gave the wrong instruction.
Shuffle the left side to ΔACB and shuffle the right side the same way, to ΔXZY. Now A goes on X, C on Z and B on Y, and the triangle lands exactly. The message is the same message, written in a new order.
The rule is to shuffle both, or neither. Several statements are right for the same pair and several are not. Read each one as an instruction and see where the triangle lands, and you never need to memorise which is which.

content.text:
A rectangle ABCD is cut along the line BD, corner to corner. The picture holds two triangles, ABD and CDB, lying together in one drawing.
Before counting anything, pull the two triangles apart. Drag each one off the other and look at them separately. Then nothing hides behind anything else.
Two pairs of sides come from the rectangle, because opposite sides of a rectangle are equal. AB is equal to CD, and AD is equal to CB.
The third side is BD. It is a side of both triangles, the very same line, so it is equal to itself. Nobody has to be told. A side that belongs to both triangles is called a free side.
Now write the match. Chintu tries A with C, B with B and D with D. Follow it. AB lands on CB, and one of those sides is long and one is short, so one end hangs over. That matching fails.
The matching that works is A with C, B with D and D with B. So triangle ABD is congruent to triangle CDB, and that one lands exactly.

content.q_figure: A rectangle ABCD cut along the diagonal BD into triangles ABD and CDB, beside a two-column table that pairs A with C, B with B and D with D.

steps: Follow A with C and B with B. That lays side AB onto side CB.
AB and CB are not equal, so one hangs over and the matching does not fit.
Start from the sides instead. AB is equal to CD, AD is equal to CB and BD is equal to DB, so A lands on C, B lands on D and D lands on B.
Write the corners in that order: triangle ABD is congruent to triangle CDB.
content.answer: No, that matching lays AB onto CB and those sides are not equal. The correct correspondence is A with C, B with D, D with B, so triangle ABD ≅ triangle CDB. Shuffling both names the same way, for example ADB ≅ CBD, says the same thing.

content.book_number: Writing the Match: the right correspondence
content.text:
$1$. Follow A with $C$ and $B$ with $B$. That lays side $AB$ onto side $CB$.
$2$. $AB$ and $CB$ are not equal, so one hangs over and the matching does not fit.
$3$. Start from the sides instead. $AB$ is equal to $CD$, $AD$ is equal to $CB$ and $BD$ is equal to $DB$, so A lands on $C$, $B$ lands on $D$ and $D$ lands on $B$.
$4$. Write the corners in that order: triangle $ABD$ is congruent to triangle $CDB$.
Answer: No, that matching lays $AB$ onto $CB$ and those sides are not equal. The correct correspondence is A with $C$, $B$ with $D$, $D$ with $B$, so triangle $ABD \cong$ triangle $CDB$. Shuffling both names the same way, for example $ADB \cong CBD$, says the same thing.

maths_rules: The kite has A at the top, B on the left, D on the right and C at the bottom. AB equals AD, marked with one bar on each, and CB equals CD, marked with two bars on each. The diagonal AC is drawn dashed. No number or length appears.
Cutting along AC gives triangle ABC on the left in teal and triangle ADC on the right in amber, with a clear gap between them. AC is drawn once in each triangle.
The third pair, AC with AC, is marked with three bars and lit green only after some students's slip and the stop.
Three sides match, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC by side side side. The statement is written with A on A, B on D and C on C.
Because the triangles are twins, angle BAC equals angle DAC and angle BCA equals angle DCA. The angle at A is cut in half only after the stop.
some students's claim fails because the shared side is a side of both triangles, so the third match is already there.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the book question, in the hook): A kite has two lines drawn inside it. Before anything is moved, which line should we cut along to get two triangles? If the child needs it rephrased: which line splits the kite into exactly two pieces? Answer: the line from eigh to C, the dashed one. Also accept: A C, the dashed one, the diagonal, top to bottom, eigh to C. If stuck: Which line splits the kite into exactly two pieces, with no bits left over? If wrong (B D): That would work too, for a different pair of triangles, but the ticks we have been given are all round eigh and C. Follow the ticks. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): Two sides matched. Where does the third match come from? Answer: A C, it is in both triangles. Also accept: A C, the shared side, it is in both, free side, the one we cut along. If stuck: Look at both triangles. Which side appears in both of them? If wrong (a side from one triangle only): That side is in the left triangle only. Look for the one that is in both. Stop 3 (after the triangles are shown to be twins): Does A C cut the angle at eigh into two equal halves? Answer: yes. Also accept: yes, yeah, it cuts it in half, two equal halves. If stuck: The triangles are twins. So what do we know about the angle at eigh in each one? If wrong (no, we would have to measure): We would, if we did not already know they were twins. But we do. It is free from the twins. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): A kite has corners P, Q, R and S, with P Q equal to P S and R Q equal to R S, and a line P R. Which side is the free side? Answer: P R. Also accept: P R, the line we cut along, the shared side, the middle line. If stuck: Pull the two triangles apart in your head. Which side did you have to draw twice? If wrong (P Q): P Q is in one triangle only. Look for the side that is in both. Watch for M6: a child who cannot find the third match is asked, have you pulled them apart? The arrowhead and the order of the corners (M5) come in the question video that follows.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the told column is filled): The question gave us two facts. Which column does the line from eigh to C, which is in both triangles, belong in? Answer: free. Also accept: free, the free one, the right one, the right column, free side. If stuck: Did the question tell you that, or did you spot it yourself? If wrong (told): Read the question again. It mentions eigh B, eigh D, C B and C D. It never says a word about eigh C. You found that one. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): Do we have to measure to know that angle B eigh C equals angle D eigh C? Answer: no, it is free from the twins. Also accept: no, free, they are twins, they are equal already, free from twins. If stuck: The two triangles land exactly on each other. Where does angle B eigh C land? If wrong (yes, measure): We could, and you would be right, but the twins have already done that work. A matching part of twins is free. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): Triangle K L M is congruent to triangle X Y Z. Which angle of triangle X Y Z must equal angle M? Answer: angle Z, and it needs no measuring, it is free from the twins. Also accept: Z, angle Z, the one matching M, no measuring, free. If stuck: The letters are written in matching order. Which letter in X Y Z sits where M sits in K L M? After the answer, ask whether it needs measuring. If wrong (angle X or angle Y): Line the two names up, K with X, L with Y, M with what? Watch for M7: a child who starts to measure parts of triangles already known to be twins is asked, what did we already prove? Watch for M6: a child who misses the shared side is asked which line they would have to draw twice if the triangles were pulled apart. The last two free facts are only named here, they are used in later topics, and the video does not teach them.

media.title: Pull Them Apart
media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'Pulling Two Triangles Apart', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
The student faces a crowded picture on the left of a stage: a kite, an arrowhead, an X of crossed lines or a rectangle with a diagonal, with the given facts printed beneath it in plain words, for example AB = AD and CB = CD. In the centre is the bench, two empty dashed outlines. On the right is a two-column sheet headed what the question tells and what comes free. Along the bottom is a palette of one, two and three bars, a single and a double angle arc and a right-angle square, with a match meter of three empty slots above the bench.

The student predicts how many matches the two triangles will give, then drags a closed triangle out of the tangle. It lifts away, leaves a ghost behind so nothing is lost, and settles in the teal outline; the second goes to the amber one. Undo or return puts a triangle back. The student taps a palette mark and then a side or angle, and must do the same on its partner in the other triangle, because a mark is never copied across: matching is the student's job. Each fact lands in the right column of the sheet by itself. When the same symbol sits on a side or angle in both triangles a slot fills green: 'Match. Two to go.' A mark on one triangle only says nothing, and the meter simply does not fill. Marking the shared side on both copies gives 'Free side. You spotted it yourself, the question never said.' At three, a rule menu opens (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS, none of these). On these cards the matches are sides, and a rule that does not fit the marks gets 'Are they three sides, or a mixture?'

Card 1 has triangle RED and triangle JAM already apart, with three pairs of equal sides. Card 2 is the kite with AB = AD, CB = CD and the diagonal AC: triangles ABC and ADC give two given matches and the free side AC. Card 3 asks what AC does to the angle at A. The twins are known, so the angle at A in one triangle equals the angle at A in the other, and AC cuts it in two equal parts, which the sheet files as free. Card 4 is the arrowhead with DF = DG, FE = GE and the line DE, and card 5 asks for its congruence: write it opens six letter slots, and F lands on G while D and E land on themselves. Card 6 is the rectangle with the diagonal BD. Card 7 shows two triangles sharing a side with one other fact given: the meter stops at two, and the student presses not enough with the reason that two matches give no way to a third.

Hints ask which side the finger traces twice, once in each triangle; then whether both columns are filled in; then whether the three matches are sides or angles. Free play adds twelve tangles, such as an hourglass of crossed lines. Through doing, the student learns that pulling the triangles apart and marking them makes a tangled picture easy, that a shared side is equal to itself, and that three matches that fit a rule make twins while two do not.

screen: A white stage in three zones.

Left zone, the tangle: one compound figure such as a kite, an arrowhead, an X of crossed lines or a rectangle with a diagonal. The given facts are printed beneath it in plain words, for example AB = AD and CB = CD.

Centre zone, the bench: two empty dashed outlines side by side. The child drags any closed triangle out of the tangle; it lifts away, leaves a ghost behind so nothing is lost, and settles into an outline, the left one in teal and the right one in amber.

Right zone, the two-column sheet, headed what the question tells and what comes free, both empty. Every fact the child marks lands in the correct column automatically, so the sheet is a record of what the child did.

Along the bottom, the marking palette: one bar, two bars, three bars, a single angle arc, a double angle arc and a right-angle square. The child taps a mark, then taps a side or angle on either separated triangle. A mark on one triangle is never copied to the other: matching is the child's job.

The match meter: a row of three empty slots. Each time the child marks the same symbol on a side or angle in both triangles, a slot fills green. At three, a rule menu appears: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS, none of these.

content.text: What can you do to a crowded picture so that two twin triangles become easy to see? Say what you think before you try it: if you redraw the two triangles of a kite apart from each other, will it be easier or harder to see which sides match? Draw a kite on your own paper with AB = AD and CB = CD, and draw the line AC. Mark one bar on AB and AD, and two bars on CB and CD. Try to find the matching sides by looking at the kite as it stands. Say how many you can find, and how sure you feel. Now redraw triangle ABC and triangle ADC far apart, and put the same bars on both copies. Look for a side that you had to draw twice. Count the matches on the separated pair. Say how many there are, and which side was the free one.

content.text:
Many figures hide two triangles in one picture, and the lines run over each other. The hard part is not the reasoning. It is the seeing. So use the same three moves every time.
Move one: pull them apart. Redraw the two triangles separately, far enough apart that nothing touches. Move two: mark what you know. Put the ticks and arcs on both copies, and include the free side. Move three: count. Are there three matches, and which three?
Try it on a kite. A is at the top, B on the left, D on the right and C at the bottom, and the line AC joins the top to the bottom. Cut along AC and pull the halves apart: triangle ABC on the left, triangle ADC on the right.
Now mark what you were told. AB equals AD, so one bar on each. CB equals CD, so two bars on each. The third match is AC. It is in both triangles, because it is the line you cut along, and a side that belongs to both is called a free side. Three sides match, so the triangles are congruent.
Because the triangles are twins, every matching part is equal for free. Angle BAC equals angle DAC, so AC cuts the top angle into two equal halves. It cuts the bottom angle in halves too, and nobody measured either.
Last, the way you write it. In an arrowhead with D at the top, E below it, F at the bottom left and G at the bottom right, DF equals DG and FE equals GE, and DE is the free side.
Triangle DFE and triangle DGE are twins. Written as triangle DFE and triangle GED, D would land on G and a long side would land on a short one. The triangles are congruent, and that sentence is still the wrong way to write it.

content.text:
Once two triangles are congruent, what can be said about the parts that match?

2. No measuring is needed for these parts: they go in the free column of the sheet.

That lays $DF$, which has one bar, onto $GE$, which has two bars, so the sides do not match and it lands crooked.
Match the sides first. $D$ goes on $D$, $F$ goes on $G$ and $E$ goes on $E$, so the right statement is triangle $DFE$ and triangle $DGE$, which can also be written triangle $FED$ and triangle $GED$.
content.answer_tex: The triangles are congruent by side side side: $DF = DG$, $FE = GE$ and $DE$ is shared. The sentence triangle $DFE$ and triangle $GED$ is not the right way to write it. The right way is triangle $DFE$ congruent to triangle $DGE$.

video_script.anchor: Which two triangles are twins, and how is it written?
video_script.design: One idea: congruent and correctly written are two questions, and a tangled figure is pulled apart first. It assumes the child has seen the three moves and the free side in the concept video. The wrong idea is some students's: any order of letters will do. The anchor question stays up from the hook; one clear, at the part boundary before the arrowhead. Meera and Rabia do not appear.

video_script.wrong_move: some students sees that the three numbers match and writes the corners in any order; read letter by letter his sentence puts the corner between three and a half and five on the corner between five and six, so it lands crooked.
maths_rules: Triangle RED has RE = 3.5, ED = 5 and DR = 6. Triangle JAM has JA = 3.5, AM = 5 and MJ = 6. The three sides match one to one, so by side side side the triangles are congruent.

The correspondence is R to J, E to A and D to M: R sits between 3.5 and 6 and so does J, E sits between 3.5 and 5 and so does A, D sits between 5 and 6 and so does M. So triangle RED is congruent to triangle JAM.

some students's sentence triangle RED congruent to triangle JMA puts E on M and D on A: E sits between 3.5 and 5 but M sits between 5 and 6, so unequal sides are laid on each other and it lands crooked.
The arrowhead has D at the top, E below it, F bottom left and G bottom right, with DF = DG (one bar) and FE = GE (two bars); DE belongs to both triangles, so it is the free side and the third match.
Three sides match in the arrowhead, so triangle DFE is congruent to triangle DGE by side side side.

The sentence triangle DFE and triangle GED puts D on G, F on E and E on D: DF (one bar) lies on GE (two bars), unequal sides, so the tracing lands crooked. The right sentence is triangle DFE and triangle DGE, equivalently triangle FED and triangle GED.
No measured length is claimed beyond the given numbers and bars: the verdicts come from matching given sides, never from measuring the picture.
video_script.payoff_line: Three matching sides make twins

final_answer.value: Congruent by SSS: sides 3.5, 5, 6 in both; triangle RED is congruent to triangle JAM, and the arrowhead pair is congruent but must be written triangle DFE and triangle DGE
final_answer.spoken: both pairs are congruent by side side side, and the corners must be written in the order they land

video_script.substitution: Match the sides first, then write the corners in the order they land: first on first, second on second, third on third.
video_script.wrong_answer: The numbers match, so I can write the letters in any order

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): Triangle RED has sides three and a half, five and six. Triangle JAM has sides six, three and a half and five. Are they congruent? Answer: yes, congruent, by side side side. Also accept: yes, congruent, side side side, twins. If stuck: Line the three numbers up against the other three. If wrong (no): Check the numbers side by side, three and a half with three and a half, five with five, six with six. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): What do you find when you line the three numbers up? Answer: the same three numbers, three and a half, five and six, in both triangles. Also accept: they match, they are the same, same numbers, all three match. If stuck: Put three and a half against three and a half, then five against five. What is left for the last pair? If wrong (they are different): Look again. The triangle on the left has three and a half, five and six. So does the one on the right. Stop 3 (after the arrowhead is pulled apart and marked): Which side is the free side in the arrowhead? Answer: D E. Also accept: D E, E D, the middle one, D to E, the one in both. If stuck: Pull the two triangles apart in your head. Which side did you have to draw twice? If wrong (D F): D F is in the left triangle only. Look for the one that is in both. Watch for M5: a child who says yes, congruent, has given half the answer. Both are needed: the triangles are congruent, and the sentence in the question puts D on G, which is the wrong way to write it. The right sentence is triangle D F E and triangle D G E, or equally triangle F E D and triangle G E D. Watch for M6: a child stuck on the arrowhead is asked one thing first, have you pulled them apart? Honesty note: the verdict on the arrowhead is reasoning from the given bars, never a measurement. The first pair is solved by matching the three numbers and then the position of each corner.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Show that zooming in makes every side longer while every angle stays exactly the same, so a child can see why equal angles do not give equal triangles. This is the rescue picture for a child who thinks the same angles make the same triangle.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first figure of a pair, amber #E69F00 for the second, green #009E73 for a matched pair of parts, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the part being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines, arcs and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a failed match or an impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. One panel on a white background, 1456 by 816. Two phones held in two hands, left and right, with a large grey magnifying glass between them. One line of text runs across the bottom of the frame. Flat illustration, thin dark outlines, flat fills.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly 2 phones, one on the left and one on the right, each held in a hand.
- The left screen shows a small triangular road sign far away, with 30 degrees, 70 degrees and 80 degrees floating at its three corners in the focus colour, and the side reading 2 cm at the bottom.
- The right screen shows the same road sign zoomed in so that it fills the screen, with the identical 30 degrees, 70 degrees and 80 degrees at its corners, and the side reading 14 cm at the bottom.
- The two triangles have the same shape: the same angles at the same corners, one small and one large.
- One large grey magnifying glass sits between the two phones.
- One line of text in green runs across the bottom of the frame.

Visible text:
- 30°
- 70°
- 80°
- side: 2 cm
- side: 14 cm
- The angles don't change when you make it bigger. The sides do.

Critical rejection conditions:
- different angle values on the two screens, because the angles must be identical
- the two triangles drawn with different shapes, so that the zoomed one is stretched
- any orange or muted red anywhere in the picture, because nothing here fails
- extra words or numbers beyond the six labels, or the words congruent or twins
- any logo or brand mark on the phones or anywhere else in the frame
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle
- tick marks that do not match the equal sides and angles stated, or a pair of figures that is not congruent when the picture says it is

Student takeaway: Zooming in changes the sides but never the angles.

video_script.design: One idea: equal angles fix the shape but not the size, so three angles cannot pin a triangle down. It assumes the child met the three sides rule and the angle sum of a triangle. media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the folded hook, on the far shot): Three sides were enough to pin a triangle down. Do you think three angles will be enough too? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: anything at all, including yes, no, maybe, I do not know. If stuck: Just say what feels right. We are about to find out either way. If wrong (what the child says): none, a prediction cannot be wrong; if the child says yes, say that is what almost everyone says and it is a completely sensible thing to think, so let us test it. Stop 2 (after the third angle fills in): I chose forty degrees and sixty-five degrees. Did I have to choose the third angle? Answer: no, it is forced. Also accept: no, it is one hundred and eighty minus the others, it works itself out, no it is forced. If stuck: What do the three angles of a triangle add up to? If wrong (yes): Try it. Forty and sixty-five are fixed. Is there any value the third angle could be other than seventy-five? Stop 3 (after Chintu's slip and the tracing): Are the three triangles twins? Answer: no. Also accept: no, not twins, different sizes, no not congruent. If stuck: Twins need the same shape and the same size. Which one is missing? If wrong (yes, Chintu's idea): Watch the tracing paper land on the big one. Does it cover it? Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): A set square has angles forty-five, forty-five and ninety degrees. A bigger one on the board has the same three angles. Are the two set squares twins? Answer: no, same shape but not the same size, so they are not congruent. Also accept: no, shape not size, they fix the shape, different sizes, the bigger one is not a twin. If stuck: Look at the zoom again. What stayed the same and what grew? If wrong (yes): Same angles only mean the same shape. Would the small one land on the big one? Folded hook: The phone and the road sign open this video, the zoom comes just after the prediction, and its one prediction question, will three angles be enough, is the first stop. Watch for M3: a child who insists that equal angles make a twin is handed the impossible card of the Shortest List tool and invited to prove it to themselves. The word similar is only named here, as next year's word, and the Flow's say-it-back about what angles fix and what they do not fix is carried by the recap line and the your-turn question. The book numbers are not reused: the video uses forty, sixty-five and seventy-five degrees.

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Give the question what is the one thing you would have to be told something to point at. Four real hinged objects are each shown half open, so a child sees that the arms stay fixed and one thing, how far open, is left to say.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first figure of a pair, amber #E69F00 for the second, green #009E73 for a matched pair of parts, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the part being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines, arcs and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a failed match or an impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Flat illustration on a white background, thin dark outlines, flat fills. Four hinged objects stand in a row, each half open: a pair of scissors, a folding wooden ruler, a drawing compass, and a door on its hinge seen from above. Each has a pink dot at its pivot. One line of text runs under all four.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly 4 objects in a row: a pair of scissors, a folding wooden ruler, a drawing compass and a door on its hinge seen from above.
- Each object is shown half open, with one dot at its pivot.
- No angle is marked and no number or arrow appears anywhere in the frame.
- One line of text runs under all four objects, and no other words are in the frame.

Visible text:
- The arms stay the same length.

Critical rejection conditions:
- any angle drawn as an arc or written as a number
- a label that says what the missing information is, such as how far open
- an object shown fully closed or fully open
- a pivot dot missing from any of the four objects
- any brand name or logo on the scissors, compass, ruler or door
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle
- tick marks that do not match the equal sides and angles stated, or a pair of figures that is not congruent when the picture says it is

video_script.design: One idea: two arms and the opening between them fix the closing side, so the triangle is fixed. It assumes the child has met congruent, the three sides rule and the angle as an opening. The wrong idea is some students's: four equal triangles show the angle does not matter. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap.
