video_script.wrong_move: some students sees four identical triangles and decides that the opening of the arms has no part in it, forgetting that all four friends chose the same opening.
maths_rules: The scissors have arms AB = 6 cm and AC = 5 cm with the pivot at A and the angle at A equal to 30 degrees. The dashed closing side is BC.
BC squared = 6 squared + 5 squared - 2 x 6 x 5 x cos 30 = 36 + 25 - 51.96 = 9.04, so BC = 3.006 cm, about 3 cm. The screen reads about 3 cm and the narration says about three centimetres.
Four friends each build 6 cm, 5 cm and 30 degrees. The four triangles are identical and land exactly on each other, so each closing side is about 3 cm.

some students's claim, that the angle cannot matter, fails because the four friends all used the same opening of 30 degrees. With the arms fixed at 6 cm and 5 cm, the closing side is about 1.38 cm at 10 degrees and about 7.11 cm at 80 degrees, so a different opening gives a different closing side.
Given: triangle ABC and triangle XYZ, with AB = XY = 6 cm, AC = XZ = 5 cm and angle A = angle X = 30 degrees. To prove: they are congruent.

Proof by moving: slide XYZ so X sits on A; turn it (and flip it if needed) so XY lies along AB; the equal angles put XZ along AC; the equal lengths put Y on B and Z on C; one straight line joins B and C, so YZ lands on BC.
The included angle is the one between the two given sides. In the letters S, A, S the angle is in the middle. No other order is shown in this video.
your turn: two triangles each with arms of 10 cm and 9 cm and an angle of 45 degrees between them; they are congruent by side angle side; the video stops before the answer.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (before the four cut-outs are stacked): Four friends each use an arm of six, an arm of five and thirty degrees between them. Will their four triangles be the same, or different? Answer: the same. Also accept: same, the same one, congruent, identical, twins. If stuck: Could any of them have drawn it differently, with those three instructions? If wrong (different): Have a look, four triangles are about to land on top of each other. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): If I open the scissors wider but keep both arms the same, what happens to the dashed side? Answer: it gets longer. Also accept: longer, it grows, bigger, gets bigger. If stuck: Open your own fingers wide and then narrow. Watch the gap between the tips. If wrong (shorter): Try it with your hand, open wide first, then narrow. Which way round is it? Stop 3 (after the rule is named): In the order side, angle, side, where does the angle sit? Answer: in the middle. Also accept: middle, in between, the middle one, between the two sides. If stuck: Read the three letters out loud: S, A, S. If wrong (at the end or the start): Say the three words slowly, side, angle, side. Which word is in the middle? Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two friends each make a triangle with arms of ten and nine centimetres and forty-five degrees between them. Are their triangles congruent? Answer: yes, two sides and the angle between them leave the third side no choice. Also accept: yes, same, yes side angle side, yes the same two sides and the same angle. If stuck: Is the angle between the two arms? What could still change? If wrong (no, we need the third side): The third side has no choice once the two arms and the opening are set, so you do not need to measure it. Watch for M9: the word included is planted here on purpose, because the next concept removes it and a child who never heard the word cannot feel its absence. The third side about three centimetres is 3.006 by calculation, so say about, never exactly.

video_script.anchor: Do two sides and an angle always make twins?
video_script.design: One idea: when the angle is not between the two sides, the loose side can swing to two places, so the same measurements give two triangles. It assumes the child met two sides with the angle between them. The wrong idea is some students's: two sides and any angle are enough. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap.

the answer to the your-turn question: no, the loose side can land in two places
video_script.wrong_move: some students thinks any two sides and any angle pin a triangle down, as they did before; the same three measurements are then drawn twice and give two triangles of different shapes.
maths_rules: The base PQ is 6 cm, the angle at P is 30 degrees, and the loose side from Q is 4 cm, so the angle is at P and the 4 cm side does not touch P.
The shortest way down from Q to the line l is 6 x sin 30 = 3 cm. The loose side of 4 cm is longer than 3 cm, so it reaches the line, and shorter than 6 cm, so it reaches it in two places.

The arc centred on Q with radius 4 cm cuts the line l at R, 2.55 cm from P, and at S, 7.84 cm from P. Triangle PQR is teal and triangle PQS is amber, drawn on the same base, and they are visibly different: one squat, one stretched out.

Both triangles have PQ = 6 cm, angle P = 30 degrees and a side of 4 cm from Q, so both obey every instruction. The measurements PR = 2.55 cm and PS = 7.84 cm are shown only after the two triangles are drawn.
some students's claim, two sides and an angle are enough so they must be twins, fails because two different triangles are drawn from the same three measurements.
The honest footnote is spoken, not written as a rule: sometimes the gate lands only once and then the triangle is pinned down, but the child would have to check every time.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the rough diagram is drawn): Look where the marked angle sits. Is it between the two sides we were given? Answer: no. Also accept: no, not included, it is at the other end, no it is away from them. If stuck: Put your finger on the six centimetre side and on the four centimetre side. Is the marked angle squeezed between your two fingers? If wrong (yes): Trace the two given sides with your finger. The thirty degrees is at P, and the four centimetre side does not touch P at all. Stop 2 (after the arc has swung): The arc has just swung. How many places did it cut the line? Answer: two. Also accept: 2, two, twice, R and S. If stuck: Count the labelled dots on the slanted line. If wrong (one): There is one low down and one further up. Watch the arc sweep again. Stop 3 (after Chintu's slip and the two triangles): Both triangles obey all three instructions. Do two sides and an angle that is not between them always give twins? Answer: no. Also accept: no, it does not, no there are two answers, not always. If stuck: You have two different triangles obeying the same instructions. Can a rule allow that? If wrong (yes, Chintu's idea): We just drew two completely different triangles from the same three numbers. A rule cannot allow two answers. Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two triangles each have a side of nine centimetres and a side of five centimetres, and an angle of twenty-five degrees at the end of the nine centimetre side, not between the two sides. Must the two triangles be twins? Answer: no, not necessarily, because the loose side can land in two places. Also accept: no, not necessarily, it depends where the angle is, the gate can land twice, not always. If stuck: Is the angle squeezed between the two sides you were given? If wrong (yes): Two sides and an angle is only enough when the angle is between the sides. Is it here? Watch for M4: the counter is never a statement, it is the gate swinging; a child who argues is handed the Swinging Gate tool to produce the two triangles. Watch for M9: a child who mixes up the two rules is asked one question only, is the angle squeezed between the two sides you were given? Honest footnote: the video says the gate sometimes lands only once and then the triangle is pinned, but you would have to check every time, and a rule you have to check is not a rule. The lengths that give none, one or two landings come back in the next concept. Checked numbers: the shortest way down from Q to the line is three centimetres, the landings are two point five five and seven point eight four centimetres from P. The your-turn numbers are checked too: nine times sine of twenty-five is about three point eight, so five centimetres is longer than that and shorter than nine, which gives two landings.

media.title: Swinging Gate
media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'What Fails and What Works', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
The student looks at a horizontal base PQ in teal, with P at the left and a long grey ray leaving P at the set angle. At Q hangs a side with a round hinge pin, the gate. A dashed reach line runs from Q straight down to the ray with its length printed, so the student sees how long the gate must be to reach at all. Three dials on the left set the base PQ from 3 to 10 centimetres, the angle at P from 10 to 150 degrees and the gate length from 1 to 12 centimetres in half-centimetre steps. One big lever, SWING, sits below them, a large landing counter reads 0, 1 or 2, and a tray at the bottom holds up to two built triangles.

Before each swing the student predicts how many places the gate can land on the ray: none, one or two. SWING sweeps the gate slowly through its arc and leaves a grey trail. Each time the tip touches the ray, a dot drops and stays. Tapping a dot builds that triangle in the tray, and COMPARE lays one over the other. For base 6, angle 30 and gate 4 there are two landings, about 2.55 and 7.84 centimetres from P, and the triangles do not match: 'Same three measurements. Different triangles.' CLEAR wipes the dots, and NO LANDING lets the student declare that the gate cannot reach.

Card 1 swings that gate of 4 and counts two. Card 2 builds both and puts one on the other. Card 3 shortens the gate to 2.5: 'It never reached,' and the reach line, 3 centimetres, shows why. Card 4 sets exactly 3 and swings very slowly: it just touches, one landing. Cards 5 and 6 set the gate to 6, the same as the base, and to 7. Each gives one landing, because the other swing position falls on P or behind it, where no triangle forms. In card 7 the angle switch moves the angle from P to Q, between the two sides; the gate is pinned and every length tried gives one landing. Card 8 asks for two landings with the angle at Q. The student presses impossible and picks the reason: with the angle between them, the two sides are pinned at both ends and nothing is left to swing.

Hints ask whether the angle is squeezed between the two sides given; then how far Q is from the ray, which is the reach line; then which gate lengths gave two landings so far. Free play unlocks every dial and a trail mode that keeps the dots of every swing, with a tally of gate lengths tried, so the student maps the lengths that give none, one or two. Through doing, the student learns that two sides and the angle between them force one triangle, that two sides and an angle not between them can leave two, and that the number of landings depends on the length of the gate.

tool_config.doer: A base PQ, a long ray from P at an angle you choose, and a gate hinged at Q. Set the base, the angle and the gate length, then pull SWING and count the landings on the ray. Tap a landing to build its triangle. Switch the angle to Q to see what changes. Afterwards, map every gate length freely.

content.text:
Three sides were enough to pin a triangle down. It is natural to think three angles will be enough too, so make a guess first and then test it.
Point a camera at a triangular road sign and read its three angles: thirty, seventy and eighty degrees. Now zoom in. The sign gets much bigger, and the three angles do not change at all.
Draw it on paper. Make thirty degrees at one end of a base and seventy degrees at the other. The two lines meet, and the third angle is whatever is left, eighty degrees. You did not choose it.
Nobody said how long the base must be. A short base gives a small triangle, a longer base gives a bigger one, and a longer base still gives an even bigger one. All of them have thirty, seventy and eighty degrees.
Trace the smallest triangle and drop the tracing on the biggest. It covers only part of it, so they are not twins. Shapes like these are called similar, a word for next year.
The angles do not change when you make it bigger. The sides do. So the angles fix the shape, and they can never tell you the size.

content.text:
Instead of measuring three sides, can the three angles recreate the triangle exactly? Try angles of 30, 70 and 80 degrees.
1. Draw a base of any length. Make an angle of 30 degrees at one end and 70 degrees at the other, and let the two lines meet at the top.
2. The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, so the third angle is 180 - 30 - 70 = 80 degrees. It is forced, not chosen.
3. The base was never fixed. Draw it short, longer and longest, and each time the angles are 30, 70 and 80 degrees.
4. The three triangles have the same shape but different sizes, so a tracing of the smallest does not land on the largest.
5. So many triangles fit these three angles and they are not congruent. Angles alone do not pin the triangle down.
Answer: No. Many triangles of different sizes have angles of 30, 70 and 80 degrees, so three angles are not enough to recreate a triangle exactly.

content.text:
This is the signboard from the start of the chapter, grown up. Two arms met at an elbow, the angle was written down, and the symbol had no choice. Now that arrangement gets a name.
Think of a pair of scissors. Two arms are joined at a pivot. The arms never change length, but you can open them as wide as you like.
Take an arm of 6 cm and an arm of 5 cm joined at a point A, and open them to 30 degrees. Join the two far tips with a straight line. That line is the third side, and a triangle appears.
Open the arms wider and the closing side gets longer. Squeeze them and it gets shorter. One opening gives one closing side, so there is no choice anywhere.
Four children each build 6 cm, 5 cm and 30 degrees. All four triangles land exactly on one another, and the closing side is about 3 cm for everybody. By calculation it is 3.006 cm.
Two sides and the angle between them make a triangle that cannot be drawn in more than one way. We call this rule S A S, for side, angle, side. The A sits in the middle of the letters because the angle sits between the two sides.
The angle between the two sides you measured has a name: the included angle. Hold on to that word, because it is about to matter a great deal.

content.text:
Two triangles have AB = XY = 6 cm, AC = XZ = 5 cm and angle A = angle X = 30 degrees. Are they congruent? Construct a triangle with these measurements and compare it with the triangles your classmates draw.
1. Draw AB = 6 cm. At A, measure 30 degrees from AB and draw AC = 5 cm along that line.
2. Join B and C. The closing side BC is about 3 cm, and calculation gives 3.006 cm.
3. Everyone who follows these three instructions gets the same BC, because the two arms and the opening between them leave only one place for the tips.
4. Lay a tracing of one triangle over another: they land exactly. There cannot be a non-congruent triangle with these measurements.
5. The rule is called S A S, side, angle, side. The angle sits between the two sides, so it is the included angle.
Answer: Yes. Two sides and the angle between them fix the triangle, so the two triangles are congruent. The closing side is about 3 cm for every child.

Draw a base of six centimetres. At one end make an angle of thirty degrees and run a long line out from it. Open your compass to four centimetres, put the point on the other end of the base and swing an arc across the line. Count the places where the arc crosses the line. Join each one to both ends of the base. Trace one triangle and try to drop the tracing on the other. Does it land?

content.text:
One word changes. Before, the angle was between the two given sides. Now it is not between them. Ask whether a rule that looked the same still works.
Draw a base PQ of six centimetres. At P make an angle of thirty degrees and run a long line l out from P. The corner R must lie somewhere on that line.
The third side is four centimetres and starts at Q. Open a compass to four centimetres, put the point on Q and swing an arc. The arc cuts the line l twice, at R and at S.
Triangle PQR and triangle PQS both have a side of six, an angle of thirty degrees and a side of four. One is squat and one is stretched out, so they are not twins.
Think of the four centimetre side as a gate hinged at Q. As it swings it touches the line in two places, 2.55 centimetres and 7.84 centimetres from P.
Two sides and an angle that is not between them is called SSA. It does not guarantee twins. Sometimes the gate reaches the line only once, but you must check every time, and a rule you must check is not a rule.

content.text:
Construct a triangle with PQ = 6 cm, the angle at P equal to 30 degrees and a side of 4 cm from Q. The angle is not between the two given sides. Can there be triangles that are not congruent with these measurements?
1. Draw the base PQ of 6 cm, and at P make an angle of 30 degrees. Run a long line l out from P.
2. Open a compass to 4 cm, put its point on Q and swing an arc across the line l.
3. The arc cuts the line l at two different points, R and S.
4. Triangle PQR and triangle PQS both have PQ = 6 cm, an angle of 30 degrees at P and a side of 4 cm from Q.
5. The straight distance from Q down to the line l is 6 x sin 30 degrees = 3 cm. The swinging side is 4 cm, which is longer than 3 cm so it reaches the line, and shorter than 6 cm so it reaches twice, at 2.55 cm and 7.84 cm from P.
6. Two triangles that are not congruent obey all three measurements, so two sides and an angle not between them (SSA) do not guarantee congruence.
Answer: Yes. The arc cuts the line at two points, giving two different triangles with the same measurements, so SSA does not guarantee congruence. Sometimes the loose side reaches the line only once, but you cannot tell without checking.

concepts.concept_name: Swing the angle away from between
concepts.predict_first: Last time the angle sat between the two sides. This time it sits at the other end of one side. Do you think two sides and that angle still leave only one triangle?
teaching_notes: Retry answer: the distance from Q to the line is still 3 cm. Five centimetres is longer than 3 and shorter than 6, so the arc cuts the line twice and one triangle is not certain.
The check answer is not necessarily, because the 40 degrees may sit away from the two sides. If the angle were between them, one triangle would be certain.
SSA is unreliable, not useless: the loose side reaches once when it is exactly 3 cm or at least 6 cm. This sets up the later topic on the right angle and the longest side.
Do not use the word congruent as a verdict on the two triangles: they are not congruent, say different triangles.
concepts.concept_description: If the angle is not between the two sides, the loose side can swing to two different landing places. Two triangles, same measurements. So SSA is no good.

content.text:
- When the angle sits between the two given sides, the triangle is forced: exactly one triangle fits.
- When the angle is not between the two sides, the loose side can swing and land in two places, so two sides and an angle do not pin the triangle down.
- How many landings there are depends on how long the loose side is: too short and it never reaches, one length only just touches, and a longer one lands twice.

content.text: Swinging Gate: A base PQ, a long ray from P at an angle you choose, and a gate hinged at Q. Set the base, the angle and the gate length, then pull SWING and count the landings on the ray. Tap a landing to build its triangle. Switch the angle to Q to see what changes. Afterwards, map every gate length freely.
content.handover: This is the gate. You set the lengths and the angle, then swing it and count the landings. I want to know afterwards how short you could make the gate and still have it land twice.

teaching_notes: Card 4 is the quiet jewel: at exactly 3 centimetres the gate grazes the ray at one point and the angle there is a right angle. Nothing is said about it; the right angle rule comes back and names it.

Landings for base 6 and angle 30 degrees by gate length: 2.5 gives 0, 3 gives 1, 4 gives 2, 5 gives 2, 6 gives 1, 7 gives 1. At 6 the second crossing falls on P itself and makes no triangle; at 7 the second crossing is behind P.
Card 1 (gate 4) lands at 2.550 and 7.842 centimetres from P, the same two triangles as the earlier construction; the child reads only the counter.
Card 8 gives no verdict word on the wrong choices; the child is sent back to try every length and the counter never reads 2.

video_script.anchor: Can two angles and the side between them make two different triangles?
video_script.design: One idea: a base and the two angles at its ends leave the third corner one place only, because two straight lines cross once. It assumes the child can use a protractor and knows what congruent means. The wrong idea is some students's: the lines could cross again further out. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap.

video_script.wrong_move: some students thinks the two long lines could meet a second time far out, giving the corner a second place; the grey lines past the first crossing only drift further apart.
maths_rules: The base BC is 9 cm, the angle at B is 45 degrees and the angle at C is 65 degrees, both measured on the same side of BC. The angle at A is 180 - 45 - 65 = 70 degrees and is never shown or spoken.
The third corner A is where the two lines cross. Using the sine rule, AB = 9 x sin 65 / sin 70 = 8.68 cm, shown as 8.7 cm, and AC = 9 x sin 45 / sin 70 = 6.77 cm.
Three children each draw the triangle and each measures AB as 8.7 cm, so the three triangles are identical and stack exactly.
Two lines that are not parallel meet in exactly one point. The lines from B and C are not parallel because they lean towards each other, and past A they drift apart for ever.
some students's claim, that the lines might cross again, fails because two straight lines cross at most once; the dotted second corner is shown with a warning mark and is never a real crossing.
The rule is angle side angle: the side BC is between the angle at B and the angle at C, which makes it the included side. The words included side first appear on screen in the last idea beat.

Your turn: base 11 cm, angle 25 degrees at one end and angle 55 degrees at the other. The two lines cross in one place only, so every child's triangle lands on every other. The answer is never shown. These numbers are not in any book question.
video_script.payoff_line: Two angles and the included side leave the corner nowhere else to go

final_answer.value: No: the two lines cross in one place only, so a base and the two angles at its ends give exactly one triangle
final_answer.spoken: no, the two lines cross in one place only, so the corner has nowhere else to go

video_script.substitution: The two lines from the ends of the base cross in one place only, so the third corner has exactly one place.
video_script.wrong_answer: The two lines might cross again further out, so eigh could have a second place.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after Chintu's slip): How many times can two straight lines cross? Answer: once. Also accept: once, one, 1, one time, only once. If stuck: Draw two straight lines on paper with a ruler. Try to make them cross twice. If wrong (twice): Have a go on paper, two straight lines. Once they have crossed they are going away from each other for ever. Stop 2 (the rule card): In angle side angle, which letter is in the middle? Answer: S, the side. After the answer, say that it sits between the two angles. Also accept: S, the side, the side is in the middle, the side is between them. If stuck: Spell it out: angle, side, angle. Which one is sandwiched? If wrong (A): Spell it out slowly, angle, side, angle. The first and last are angles. Which is left in the middle? Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): A base is eleven centimetres with twenty-five degrees at one end and fifty-five degrees at the other. Will every child's triangle land exactly on every other child's, and what makes sure of it? Answer: yes, because the two lines from the ends of the base cross in one place only, so the corner has nowhere else to go. Also accept: yes, same triangle, they all match, one place for the corner, the lines cross once, the side is between the angles. If stuck: Draw the base and the two lines. How many places can the third corner be? If wrong (no, they could differ): Try it with your ruler and protractor. Where could a second corner go? Watch for M9: the word included is planted here and tested later, so a child who thinks any side will do is not corrected here. The question what if the side is not between the angles is deliberately left open for a later concept. The new terms are included side and angle side angle.

maths_rules: Two segments AD and BC cross at O, and O is the midpoint of both: AO = OD with one tick on each, and BO = OC with two ticks on each. The two outer edges AB and DC are drawn dotted and carry no tick and no length until the payoff.
Triangle AOB is teal and triangle DOC is amber. After the pull apart, AO and OD turn green with one tick and BO and OC turn green with two ticks; the match meter reads 2 of 3.

The free angles are angle AOB and angle DOC, the two angles facing each other at the crossing. They are shown equal with matching arcs, and the angle sits between the two equal sides in each triangle.
The congruence statement is written in matching order: triangle AOB is congruent to triangle DOC, with A on D, O on O and B on C. AB and DC are corresponding sides.
some students's idea, to measure AB and CD, is not a wrong calculation: it is only unnecessary once the triangles are twins, and the video does not measure anything.

Your turn: planks EH and FG cross at their middles at P, so EP = PH and FP = PG, and the free angles at P give side angle side for triangles EPF and HPG. EF is 19 cm, so GH is 19 cm; the answer is never shown.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the book question, after the figure is set up): Point O is the middle of both sticks. What can you say about the lengths of eigh B and C D? If the child needs it rephrased: nobody has measured the two outside edges, so what do you think about them? Answer: no right answer yet, this is a prediction; the video shows that they are equal. Also accept: equal, the same, I do not know, they might be equal, let us measure. If stuck: Look at the middle of the figure. Which parts are equal because O is the middle? If wrong (a child says they are different): Let us find out, there is a way to know without a ruler. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): Two matches so far, and nothing left in the question. Where could a third match come from? Answer: the angles where the lines cross. Also accept: the angles, where they cross, at O, vertically opposite angles, the opposite angles. If stuck: Look at the point where the two sticks cross. Is anything equal there? If wrong (measure a side): We could, but there is a fact sitting at O that nobody had to give us. Look at the angles there. Stop 3 (after the free angle is placed between two sides): Count the matches: two sides and one angle. Where does the angle sit? Answer: between the two sides, so the rule is side angle side. Also accept: between the two sides, in the middle, squeezed between them, side angle side. If stuck: Put a finger on the angle. Which two sides make that corner? After the answer, ask which rule that is. If wrong (off to one side): Look at the corner. Which two sides meet at it, eigh O and B O, or others? Stop 4 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two planks E H and F G cross at their middles at P, and E F is nineteen centimetres long. How long is G H? Answer: nineteen centimetres, because the triangles E P F and H P G are twins by side angle side and E F and H G are matching sides. Also accept: nineteen, the same as E F, equal to E F. If stuck: The triangles are twins. What does that give you, for free? If wrong (we do not know): We do now. Every matching part of twin triangles is equal. Watch for M7: a child who wants to measure eigh B and C D is asked what was already proved about the triangles. The talk image where the roads cross comes before this video and asks which two angles are equal without anybody measuring. The congruence statement is read letter by letter: eigh on D, O on O, B on C.

video_script.anchor: Are two angles and a side enough when the side is not between them?
video_script.design: One idea: when the side is not between the two given angles, work out the third angle first, because angles add to one hundred and eighty, and the side is then between two known angles. It assumes the child knows angle side angle and the angle sum. The wrong idea is some students's: not between means it fails. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap.
source: Angle, angle, side: are they congruent? Find the missing angles
never_show: the value of the third angle before the stop on it
the answer to the your-turn question: the third angle is fifty-five degrees and then the side is between two known angles
video_script.wrong_move: some students thinks that a side not between the two angles must fail, as it did for side side angle; the third angle can be worked out from the other two, so the side ends up between two known angles.
maths_rules: Triangle ABC (teal) has angle A = 35 degrees, angle C = 75 degrees and side BC = 4 cm; triangle XYZ (amber) has angle X = 35 degrees, angle Z = 75 degrees and side YZ = 4 cm. The side BC joins B and C, so it is not between the angles at A and C.

The third angle is 180 - 35 - 75 = 70 degrees, so angle B = 70 degrees, and the same sum gives angle Y = 70 degrees. 35 + 75 = 110 and 180 - 110 = 70. The value 70 is never on screen before the stop on the third angle has been answered.

After that, angle B = angle Y = 70 degrees, side BC = side YZ = 4 cm and angle C = angle Z = 75 degrees, so BC lies between the 70 degree and the 75 degree angles, which is angle side angle, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XYZ.

some students's claim, that a side not between the angles must fail like side side angle, is false: in side side angle the third side can swing to two places, while here nothing is left free once the third angle is known.
Angle angle side is a name for this condition: two angles and a side not between them. It is angle side angle after working out the third angle.

Your turn: two triangles each with angles 40 degrees and 85 degrees and a side of 7 cm that is not between them. The third angle is 180 - 40 - 85 = 55 degrees, then the side lies between two known angles, so the triangles are congruent. The answer is never shown. These numbers are not in any book question.
video_script.payoff_line: An angle you were not given is an angle you can work out

final_answer.value: Congruent: angle B = 180 - 35 - 75 = 70 degrees, and angle Y = 70 degrees likewise, so BC is between two known angles (angle side angle)
final_answer.spoken: yes, they are congruent, because the third angle can be worked out and then the side is between two known angles

video_script.substitution: Angles come in threes that add to one hundred and eighty, so the missing angle can be worked out and the side then sits between two known angles.
video_script.wrong_answer: Not between the angles, like side side angle, so it fails.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after Chintu's slip): Chintu says this is side side angle all over again, so it must fail. Is he right? Answer: no. Also accept: no, it is different, those were sides, no these are angles. If stuck: What was swinging about in the gate, a side or an angle? If wrong (yes): It is a very fair thing to think. But watch what happens next, angles can do something sides cannot. Stop 2 (the third angle): Thirty-five degrees and seventy-five degrees are two of the three angles. What is the third? Answer: seventy degrees. Also accept: 70, 70 degrees, seventy, seventy degrees. If stuck: The three angles add to one hundred and eighty. Take thirty-five and seventy-five away. If wrong (110): Careful, one hundred and ten is what the two of them add up to. Now take that away from one hundred and eighty. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two triangles each have angles of forty and eighty-five degrees. Each has a side of seven centimetres that is not between those angles. Are the two triangles congruent? Answer: yes, they are congruent, and you work out the third angle first, which is fifty-five degrees, so the side ends up between two known angles. Also accept: yes, the third angle, one hundred and eighty take away forty and eighty-five, fifty-five, angle side angle after the third angle. If stuck: Two angles are known in each triangle. What can you get from them? After the answer, ask what you work out first. If wrong (no, the side is not between): Remember the two rows. Angles give you the third for free. What does that do to the side? Watch for M9: a child who has learned that not included means it fails is corrected with a reason, the rule is not about the word included, it is about whether anything is left free to move. Watch for M8: two angles give the third is true, two sides give the third is not, and they sound alike. The new term is angle angle side. The three-angle sum is used as known.

media.title: Angle Side Angle
media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'Two Angles and a Side', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
A base lies horizontally in teal, labelled with its length, with a round grey protractor at each end. Two rays run out from the ends at the angles the protractors show, solid teal up to the crossing and grey beyond. The crossing is a bright green labelled dot that moves live, with a readout of its height above the base. On the left, three dials set the base from 2 to 12 centimetres and the left and right angles each from 5 to 170 degrees. A fourth readout shows third angle equals 180 minus left minus right, and greys out when the sum reaches 180. A sum bar fills as the angles grow, with a red line at 180 degrees. A top-angle switch, COUNT CROSSINGS and IMPOSSIBLE complete the controls.

The student first predicts whether the rays will cross once, twice or sometimes not at all, then turns the dials and watches the green dot move: 'One crossing. One triangle.' Card 1 builds a base of 5 with angles of 50 and 30 degrees. Card 2 keeps the angles and changes the base to 9: the triangle is bigger with the same shape, so it is not a twin of the first. Card 3 presses COUNT CROSSINGS, which extends both rays to the edge of the stage and marks every crossing, and the answer is always 1.

Cards 4 and 5 use the top-angle mode. The switch hides one end angle and shows the angle at the top instead, and the student must work out the missing end angle and type it into the entry box before the rays will draw. Card 4 has base 4, top angle 35 and right-hand angle 75, so the left angle is 180 minus 35 minus 75, which is 70. Card 5 has base 7, top angle 40 and left angle 60, so the right-hand angle is 80. A wrong entry gets 'Check the sum. Three angles, 180 degrees between them.' Card 6 sets both end angles to 95 degrees. The sum bar passes the red line and the rays never cross: 'Those two angles have used up the whole 180 degrees. There is nothing left for the top.' Card 7 asks for the rays to cross in two places. The student presses IMPOSSIBLE and picks the reason: two straight lines that are not parallel cross once.

Hints ask whether the base is squeezed between the two angles given; then, in top-angle mode, to find the missing end angle first; then to look at the sum bar. In free play both angle dials and the base are free, and a ghost button leaves a faint copy of every triangle built, so a family sharing one base appears, with a quiet count of triangles built. Through doing, the student learns that two angles and the side between them leave exactly one triangle, that a known side and any two angles do the same job because the third angle is what is left of 180 degrees, and that the same angles with a different side give a different size.

Start with a base BC of 5 cm. This time you are given the side first, and then the two angles at its ends.
At B, use a protractor to mark 50 degrees and draw a long ray. At C, mark 30 degrees and draw a long ray the other way. The two rays head towards each other.
They cross, and the crossing point is the third corner, A. Two straight lines that are not parallel cross once and never again, so there is exactly one place for A.
Four children each build 5 cm, 50 degrees and 30 degrees. All four triangles land exactly on one another. Nobody had a choice about where A went.
Two angles and the side between them make a triangle that cannot be drawn in more than one way. We call this rule A S A, for angle, side, angle. The S sits in the middle of the letters because the side sits between the two angles.
The side between the two angles has a name: the included side. Remember the word. The next question asks what happens when the side is not between them.

content.text:
Two triangles have BC = YZ = 5 cm, angle B = angle Y = 50 degrees and angle C = angle Z = 30 degrees. Are they congruent? Can there be triangles with these measurements that are not congruent? Construct one and find out.
1. Draw BC = 5 cm. At B, measure 50 degrees from BC and draw a long ray.
2. At C, measure 30 degrees from CB on the same side and draw a long ray. The two rays head towards each other.
3. The rays cross at one point, and that point is A. Two straight lines that are not parallel cross only once, so A has only one possible place.
4. The angle at A is 180 - 50 - 30 = 100 degrees, the same for every child, and the triangles land exactly on one another.
5. So no triangle with these measurements can differ from another. The side BC sits between the two angles, which is why the rule is called A S A.
Answer: Yes. The side and the two angles at its ends leave only one place for the third corner, so all such triangles are congruent.

content.text:
The figure is an X. Two straight lines, A to D and B to C, cross at a point O. O is the exact middle of both lines. The question is about the two outer edges, AB and CD. Nobody has measured either of them.
Pull the two triangles apart: triangle A O B and triangle D O C. Mark what is given. O is the middle of A D, so A O equals O D, one tick. O is the middle of B C, so B O equals O C, two ticks. That is two matches, and one is still missing.
The third match is sitting at the crossing. Where two straight lines cross, the angles that face each other are equal, and nobody has to tell you. These are the vertically opposite angles, and here they are the free angles. Angle A O B equals angle D O C.
Now the match is side, angle, side, with the angle between the two sides. That is the SAS rule, so triangle A O B is congruent to triangle D O C.
A B and D C are matching sides of twin triangles, so they are equal. Neither was ever measured. Matching parts of twins are equal for free.

content.text:
Last time a side that was not between the given parts spoiled everything. It is easy to learn a false rule from that: not between means it fails. That is not the reason it failed.
The real reason was that something was left free to swing. So the question to ask is: is anything left free to move?
Take two triangles with a 35 degree angle, a 75 degree angle and a 4 centimetre side. The side is along the bottom, not between the two angles.
Angles come in threes and add to 180 degrees. Know two angles and the third is not a mystery. The two given angles add to 110, so the third angle is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees.
Now the 4 centimetre side sits between the 70 degree angle and the 75 degree angle. That is the A S A rule we already trust.
So the triangles are congruent. This case has its own name, A A S, for angle, angle, side. It is really A S A after one small subtraction.
Sides do not work like that. Know two sides and the third side is still free. Two angles give the third for nothing; two sides give nothing.

content.text:
Two triangles ABC and XYZ have angle A = angle X = 35 degrees, angle C = angle Z = 75 degrees and BC = YZ = 4 cm. The side is not between the two given angles. Are the triangles congruent? Find the missing angles B and Y.
1. The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, so a third angle is 180 minus the other two.
2. The two given angles add to 35 + 75 = 110 degrees.
3. Angle B = 180 - 110 = 70 degrees, and angle Y = 70 degrees in the same way.
4. Now BC lies between angle B and angle C, and YZ lies between angle Y and angle Z.
5. Angle B = angle Y, BC = YZ and angle C = angle Z, so the triangles are congruent by A S A: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XYZ.
6. This case is called A A S, for angle, angle, side, and it guarantees congruence.
Answer: Congruent. Angle B = angle Y = 70 degrees, then A S A gives triangle ABC congruent to triangle XYZ. The A A S condition guarantees congruence.

content.text:
- A side with an angle at each end sends out two rays, and two rays that are not parallel cross in exactly one place, so exactly one triangle fits.
- Keep the angles and change the side, and you get a different triangle, bigger or smaller, with the same shape.
- When two angles of a triangle are known, the third is what is left of one hundred and eighty degrees, so a known side and any two angles do the same job.
- If the two end angles add to one hundred and eighty degrees or more, the rays never cross and there is no triangle.

concepts.concept_name: Two Angles and a Side: Q1

content.book_number: Two Angles and a Side: the midpoint figure
content.question: In the figure, O is the midpoint of AD and of BC. What can one say about the lengths AB and CD?
content.text: In the figure, $O$ is the midpoint of $AD$ and of $BC$. What can one say about the lengths $AB$ and $CD$?
content.publication_text: In the figure, $O$ is the midpoint of $AD$ and of $BC$. What can one say about the lengths $AB$ and $CD$?
content.question_tex: In the figure, $O$ is the midpoint of $AD$ and of $BC$. What can one say about the lengths $AB$ and $CD$?
content.q_figure: Two segments AD and BC crossing at O, with A at the top left, C at the top right, B at the bottom left and D at the bottom right, AB and CD joined, AO and OD marked with one tick each and BO and OC marked with two ticks each.

concepts.concept_name: Two Angles and a Side: Ans1

steps: Pull the triangles apart: triangle AOB and triangle DOC.
O is the midpoint of AD, so AO = OD. O is the midpoint of BC, so BO = OC. That is two matches.
Angle AOB and angle DOC face each other where the two lines cross, so they are vertically opposite and equal.
Two sides and the angle between them match, so by SAS triangle AOB is congruent to triangle DOC.
AB and DC are corresponding sides of twin triangles, so AB = CD.
content.answer: AB = CD. Because AO = OD, BO = OC (O is the midpoint of both) and angle AOB = angle DOC (vertically opposite), the triangles are congruent by SAS: triangle AOB is congruent to triangle DOC. AB and DC are corresponding sides, so they are equal.

content.question: Triangle ABC has AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm and angle B = 47 degrees. Triangle XYZ has XZ = 7 cm, ZY = 5 cm and angle Z = 47 degrees. Are they congruent? Which rule fits, and in what order do you write the letters?
content.text: Triangle $ABC$ has $AB = 7\text{ cm}$, $BC = 5\text{ cm}$ and angle $B = 47$ degrees. Triangle $XYZ$ has $XZ = 7\text{ cm}$, $ZY = 5\text{ cm}$ and angle $Z = 47$ degrees. Are they congruent? Which rule fits, and in what order do you write the letters?

content.q_figure: Two triangles: ABC with A at the top, B at the bottom left and C at the bottom right, AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm and the angle at B equal to 47 degrees; and XYZ with X at the top left, Y at the bottom and Z at the right, XZ = 7 cm, YZ = 5 cm and the angle at Z equal to 47 degrees.

concepts.concept_name: Two Angles and a Side: Ans2

steps: In the first triangle the 47 degree angle is at B, between the sides AB and BC.
In the second triangle the 47 degree angle is at Z, between the sides ZX and ZY. The angle is at Z, not at Y.
So B matches Z, and the sides match AB with XZ (7 cm) and BC with ZY (5 cm).
Side, angle, side with the angle between the sides is the S A S rule, so the triangles are congruent.
Write the letters in matching order: A, B, C against X, Z, Y.
content.answer: Congruent by S A S: AB = XZ = 7 cm, BC = ZY = 5 cm and angle B = angle Z = 47 degrees. Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY.

content.book_number: Two Angles and a Side: parallel lines AB and CD
content.question: In the figure, DC is parallel to AB and DC = AB, and the lines DB and AC cross at O. Which triangles are congruent, by which rule, and which other parts are then equal?
content.text: In the figure, $DC$ is parallel to $AB$ and $DC = AB$, and the lines $DB$ and $AC$ cross at $O$. Which triangles are congruent, by which rule, and which other parts are then equal?

content.q_figure: Segments DB and AC crossing at O, with D at the top left, C at the top right, A at the bottom left and B at the bottom right, DC and AB joined, drawn with parallel arrows and marked equal in length.

concepts.concept_name: Two Angles and a Side: Ans3

steps: Look at the two triangles COD and AOB that meet at O.
DC is parallel to AB, so the alternate angles are equal: angle DCO = angle BAO and angle CDO = angle ABO.
The sides DC and AB are given equal, and each sits between the two equal angles of its triangle.
Angle, side, angle is the A S A rule, so triangle COD is congruent to triangle AOB.
Once the triangles are congruent every matching part is equal, so OC = OA, OD = OB, and angle COD = angle AOB (vertically opposite).
content.answer: Congruent by A S A: triangle COD is congruent to triangle AOB. The other equal parts are OC = OA, OD = OB and angle COD = angle AOB.

content.q_figure: A four-sided figure with A at the top, B at the left, C at the right and D at the bottom, the line BC drawn across the middle, angles ABC and DBC marked with one arc each and angles ACB and DCB marked with two arcs each.

concepts.concept_name: Two Angles and a Side: Ans4

steps: Pull the two triangles apart: triangle ABC and triangle DBC.
Angle ABC = angle DBC and angle ACB = angle DCB are given.
BC belongs to both triangles, so BC = BC, and it lies between the two equal angles.
Angle, side, angle is the A S A rule, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DBC.
Matching parts of twins are equal, so angle BAC = angle BDC.
content.answer: Congruent by A S A: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DBC. So angle BAC = angle BDC.

content.question: In the figure, AC and DB cross, angle ABD = angle DCA and angle ACB = angle DBC. Show that angle ABC = angle DCB and that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DCB. Which other parts are equal?
content.text: In the figure, $AC$ and $DB$ cross, angle $ABD =$ angle $DCA$ and angle $ACB =$ angle $DBC$. Show that angle $ABC =$ angle $DCB$ and that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DCB$. Which other parts are equal?

content.question_tex: In the figure, $AC$ and $DB$ cross, angle $ABD =$ angle $DCA$ and angle $ACB =$ angle $DBC$. Show that angle $ABC =$ angle $DCB$ and that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DCB$. Which other parts are equal?
content.q_figure: Segments AC and DB crossing at O, with A at the top left, D at the top right, B at the bottom left and C at the bottom right, AB, DC and BC drawn, angles ABD and DCA marked with one arc each and angles ACB and DBC marked with two arcs each.

concepts.concept_name: Two Angles and a Side: Ans5

steps: At B the whole angle ABC is angle ABD and angle DBC added together. At C the whole angle DCB is angle DCA and angle ACB added together.
Angle ABD = angle DCA and angle DBC = angle ACB, so the two whole angles are equal: angle ABC = angle DCB.
BC is a side of both triangles, so BC = CB, and it lies between the equal angles at B and C.
Angle ACB = angle DBC is also given, so angle, side, angle holds: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DCB by A S A.
Matching parts of twins are equal: AB = DC, AC = DB and angle BAC = angle CDB.
Extra step: angle OBC = angle OCB at the crossing point O, so triangle OBC has two equal angles and OB = OC. Then OA = OD, because AC = DB.
content.answer: Angle ABC = angle DCB, and triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DCB by A S A. Equal parts: AB = DC, AC = DB, angle BAC = angle CDB. Also OB = OC, and so OA = OD.
content.question: In the figure, AC and DB cross, angle ABD = angle DCA and angle ACB = angle DBC. Show that angle ABC = angle DCB and that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DCB. Which other parts are equal?

content.book_number: Two Angles and a Side: crossing lines AC and DB
content.text:
$1$. At $B$ the whole angle $ABC$ is angle $ABD$ and angle $DBC$ added together. At $C$ the whole angle $DCB$ is angle $DCA$ and angle $ACB$ added together.
$2$. Angle $ABD =$ angle $DCA$ and angle $DBC =$ angle $ACB$, so the two whole angles are equal: angle $ABC =$ angle $DCB$.
$3$. $BC$ is a side of both triangles, so $BC = CB$, and it lies between the equal angles at $B$ and $C$.
$4$. Angle $ACB =$ angle $DBC$ is also given, so angle, side, angle holds: triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DCB$ by $A S A$.
$5$. Matching parts of twins are equal: $AB = DC$, $AC = DB$ and angle $BAC =$ angle $CDB$.
$6$. Extra step: angle $OBC =$ angle $OCB$ at the crossing point $O$, so triangle $OBC$ has two equal angles and $OB = OC$. Then $OA = OD$, because $AC = DB$.
Answer: Angle $ABC =$ angle $DCB$, and triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DCB$ by $A S A$. Equal parts: $AB = DC$, $AC = DB$, angle $BAC =$ angle $CDB$. Also $OB = OC$, and so $OA = OD$.

video_script.design: One idea: name what is given, check where it sits, then write the match in the order the corners land. It assumes the child has met side angle side and angle side angle in the concept videos. The wrong idea is some students's: letters in alphabetical order will do. The anchor question stays up from the hook; one clear at each part boundary. Meera and Rabia do not appear.

video_script.wrong_move: some students writes triangle ABC and triangle XYZ in alphabetical order; read letter by letter, B lands on Y, but the forty-seven degrees is at B and at Z, so the match lands crooked.
maths_rules: Triangle ABC has AB = 7, BC = 5 and the angle at B equal to 47 degrees, between those two sides. Triangle XZY has XZ = 7, ZY = 5 and the angle at Z equal to 47 degrees, between those two sides. Two sides and the angle between them match, so by side angle side the triangles are congruent.

The correspondence is A to X, B to Z and C to Y, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY. some students's sentence triangle ABC and triangle XYZ puts B on Y: B holds the 47 degrees between 7 and 5, but Y does not, so it lands crooked.

The hourglass has D top left, C top right, A bottom left and B bottom right, with DB and AC crossing at O, DC parallel to AB, and DC = AB marked. Alternate angles are equal, so angle CDO = angle ABO and angle DCO = angle BAO, and DC, the side between them, is equal to AB. By angle side angle, triangle COD is congruent to triangle AOB.

The kite has A at the top, B at the left, C at the right and D at the bottom, with BC horizontal. Angle ABC = angle DBC and angle ACB = angle DCB are marked. BC is in both triangles and sits between the equal angles, so by angle side angle triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DBC.

In the last picture A is top left, D is top right, B is bottom left and C is bottom right, with AC and DB crossing. Angle ABD = angle DCA and angle ACB = angle DBC are given. Angle ABC = angle ABD + angle DBC and angle DCB = angle DCA + angle ACB, so the two whole angles are equal. With BC common and angle ACB = angle DBC, angle side angle gives triangle ABC congruent to triangle DCB.
No measured length or angle is claimed beyond the given numbers and marks: every verdict comes from the given equal parts, never from measuring the picture.
video_script.payoff_line: The letters follow the equal parts

final_answer.value: First pair: congruent by SAS, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY; hourglass: ASA, triangle COD is congruent to triangle AOB; kite: ASA, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DBC, BC is the side in both; last picture: angle ABD plus angle DBC makes angle ABC, and ASA gives triangle ABC congruent to triangle DCB
final_answer.spoken: each picture fits side angle side or angle side angle, and the letters follow the equal parts

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): Both triangles have sides seven and five, and an angle of forty-seven degrees. Which rule says they are congruent? Answer: side angle side. Also accept: SAS, side angle side, the rule where the angle is between the two sides. If stuck: Count what you have got: two sides and one angle. Is the angle between them? If wrong (side side angle): Check where the forty-seven sits. Is it squeezed between the seven and the five? Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Where does the forty-seven degrees sit among the seven and the five? Answer: yes, it sits between them in both. Also accept: yes, it is between, it is in the middle, it is the corner where the seven and the five meet. If stuck: Put a finger on the forty-seven. Which two sides make that corner? If wrong (no): Look at the corner where the seven and the five meet. That is where the forty-seven sits, at B in one triangle and at Z in the other. Stop 3 (the hourglass, after the two pairs of equal angles and the sides between them): Which rule is that? Answer: angle side angle. Also accept: ASA, angle side angle. If stuck: Which two angles are equal, and where does the side D C sit? If wrong (side angle side): There are two angles and one side here. Count them again. Stop 4 (the kite, after it is pulled apart): In the kite, which side is in both triangles? Answer: B C. Also accept: B C, C B, the bottom one, the horizontal one, the one at the bottom. If stuck: Pull the kite apart along B C. Which side did you have to draw twice? If wrong (A B or D C): That side is in one triangle only. Look for the one that both triangles share. Stop 5 (the last picture): Angle A B D and angle D B C make which whole angle? Answer: angle A B C. Also accept: A B C, the whole angle at B, the big one at B, angle A B C. If stuck: The two small angles sit side by side at B. What do they make together? If wrong (angle D B C or a number): That is one of the two small angles. Put the two together and name the corner they fill. Watch for M5: a child who writes the letters in order has matched the names and not the corners. Read the statement letter by letter, first on first, second on second, third on third; here B goes on Z, not on Y. Honesty note: the verdicts come from the given equal sides and angles, never from measuring a picture. The video answers the first three pictures in full. For the last picture it stops at the whole angle and the board gives the reasoning.

media.description: Two halves. On the left, headed SSA, an arc of 4 cm cuts a 30 degree ray twice above a base of 6 cm, making two different overlapping triangles. On the right, headed RHS, a base of 4 cm with a right angle at one end and an arc of 5 cm cut the upright line above and below, making two triangles that are mirror images across a dashed fold line.
media.teaching_notes: Ask the child where the second landing is in each half. Left, on the same side of the base, so two different triangles. Right, on the other side, so the same triangle flipped. The bottom line is the summary, so show it last.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Put the two constructions next to each other so a child sees that the arc lands twice on the same side when the angle is not a right angle, and on opposite sides when it is. This is the rescue picture for a child who says a right angle cannot fix the triangle.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first figure of a pair, amber #E69F00 for the second, green #009E73 for a matched pair of parts, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the part being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines, arcs and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a failed match or an impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. One panel on a white background, 1456 by 816, split down the middle by a thin grey construction line. Flat illustration, thin dark outlines, flat fills. A headed construction on each half, a caption under each half, and one line of text across the very bottom.

Exact mathematical structure:
- The frame is split into a left half and a right half by one thin vertical grey line.
- Left half, headed SSA in the nope colour: base PQ of 6 cm, a 30 degree ray from P, and an arc of 4 cm from Q cutting the ray at R and S, both above the base.
- In the left half, triangle PQR is a pale teal fill and triangle PQS is a pale amber fill, clearly different shapes, drawn overlapping.
- Right half, headed RHS in the agree colour: base QR of 4 cm with a small square right angle mark at Q, the upright line drawn both above and below the base, and an arc of 5 cm from R cutting it at P above and P' below.
- In the right half, triangle PQR is a pale teal fill and triangle P'QR is a pale amber fill, mirror images of each other across QR.
- In the right half, a dashed green fold line runs along QR, with a curved arrow from P to P'.
- A caption sits under each half and one line of text runs across the very bottom of the frame.

Visible text:
- SSA
- RHS
- 6 cm
- 30°
- 4 cm
- 5 cm
- P
- Q
- R
- S
- P'
- Two landings, same side. Two different triangles.
- Two landings, opposite sides. One triangle, flipped.
- RHS is SSA with the second landing folded away.

Critical rejection conditions:
- both SSA landings drawn on opposite sides of the base, because they must be on the same side
- the two RHS triangles drawn as different sizes or shapes, because they must be mirror images
- the SSA triangles drawn identical, because they must be clearly different
- orange used anywhere in the right half, or green anywhere in the left half
- any extra words or numbers beyond the listed labels, or any logo or brand mark
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle
- tick marks that do not match the equal sides and angles stated, or a pair of figures that is not congruent when the picture says it is

Student takeaway: With a right angle the second landing is only a flip of the first, so there is one triangle.

video_script.anchor: Can a right angle still fix a triangle?
video_script.design: One idea: with a right angle the second landing is on the other side of the base, so it is the first triangle flipped and the triangle is fixed. It assumes the child met the swinging gate and Rabia's two circles. The wrong idea is some students's: two landings means the gate trouble again. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear, at the part boundary before the recap.
source: Right angle, long side and one more side: the arc cut twice
Right angle, hypotenuse and side
never_show: a verdict that the two triangles are different
the answer to the your-turn question: one triangle flipped over
video_script.wrong_move: some students sees the arc cut the upright line twice and says it is the gate trouble again; the paper then folds along the base and the upper point lands exactly on the lower one.
maths_rules: The first triangle has a base QR of 9 cm, a right angle at Q marked with a small square, and a long side PR of 15 cm opposite the right angle; the upright line through Q is drawn long and the compass arc of 15 cm is centred on R.
The arc cuts the upright line above the base at P and again below the base at P', and the two points are the same distance from Q; the triangle PQR is teal and the triangle P'QR is amber.
The second measured case has a base of 20 cm and a long side of 29 cm; its arc also cuts the upright line once above and once below the base, with the two landings the same distance from Q.
Folding the paper along QR sends P exactly onto P'; the two triangles are mirror images of each other and match with a flip.
The swinging gate picture shows two landings on the same side of the base, two visibly different triangles; the two landings of the right angle case are on opposite sides of the base.
The long side opposite the right angle is lit in the focus colour and named hypotenuse; no derived third side length is written anywhere in the video.
your turn: a right angle, a long side of 20 cm and a base of 12 cm; the arc lands above and below the base; the answer, one triangle flipped over, is never shown.
video_script.payoff_line: The second landing is only a flip

final_answer.value: Yes: a right angle, the hypotenuse and one more side fix the triangle, because the two landings are on opposite sides of the base and are flips of each other
final_answer.spoken: yes, a right angle, the hypotenuse and one more side fix the triangle, because the second landing is only a flip

video_script.substitution: With a right angle at the corner the second landing falls on the other side of the base, so it is the first triangle flipped over and only one triangle is left.
video_script.wrong_answer: two landings again, so it is the gate trouble all over again

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the folded hook, on the right angle at the grazing corner): The angle there reads ninety degrees, at exactly the spot where the gate stopped landing twice. Do you think that is a coincidence? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: anything at all, including yes, no, I do not know, probably not. If stuck: No right answer here. Just a hunch. If wrong (what the child says): none, a prediction cannot be wrong; say let us go and see. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip, with the arc cutting the line below the base as well): The arc has cut the line below the base as well. Is this the gate trouble all over again? Answer: no. Also accept: no, it is a flip, it is the same triangle upside down, no, mirror image. If stuck: Look at the two triangles. Are they really different shapes, or the same one reflected? If wrong (yes): Perfectly reasonable, but watch the fold. I think it will change your mind, just like it did with the two circles. Stop 3 (after the side by side picture): How are the two gate landings unlike these two landings? Answer: these two are on opposite sides of the base. Also accept: opposite sides, one is above and one is below, these are mirror images, they are flipped. If stuck: In the gate picture, were both triangles above the base or on different sides of it? If wrong (what the child says): the gate landings were different triangles; ask which side of the base each landing sits on, and point at the fold line. Stop 4 (after the naming card): In the triangle with the nine centimetre base, which side is the hypotenuse? Answer: the fifteen centimetre side, the slanted one from P to the far end of the base. Also accept: fifteen, the slanted one, the one opposite the right angle, P to the end of the base. If stuck: Which corner holds the right angle, and which side faces it? If wrong (the base or the upright line): Those two make the right angle. The hypotenuse is the side opposite it. Stop 5 (the your-turn question, at the end): A right angle, a long side of twenty centimetres and a base of twelve centimetres. The arc lands above and below the base. Are the two triangles different or the same? Answer: the same, one triangle flipped over, because the two landings are on opposite sides of the base. Also accept: same, a mirror image, one triangle, a flip, only one triangle. If stuck: Fold the paper along the base in your head. Where does the upper point go? If wrong (different): The two landings are on opposite sides of the base. Does a flip make a different triangle? Folded hook: Remember the Gate, the gate replay and the grazing right angle, opens this video as its first two beats, and its one prediction question, is the right angle a coincidence, is the first stop. Watch for M4: a child who learned that two sides and an angle never work will object that the right angle case cannot work either. Welcome it: good, you are holding me to the rule, look where the second landing is. Watch for M2: this video depends on accepting that a flip is still a twin; a child who wobbles goes back to the tracing test picture, not forward. The book numbers are not reused: the video uses nine, fifteen, twenty-nine and twenty, with twelve and twenty in the your-turn question.

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Show every condition of the topic on one wall chart: the five that guarantee congruence and the two that look as if they should and do not, each with its own small construction and a one-line reason. This is the chapter's revision sheet and a rescue picture.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first figure of a pair, amber #E69F00 for the second, green #009E73 for a matched pair of parts, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the part being asked about, grey #6B7280 for construction lines, arcs and grids, muted red #D55E00 only for a failed match or an impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. One panel on a white background, 1456 by 816. A wall chart with seven rows and four cells in each: the code in large letters, a small accurate thumbnail construction, a tick or a cross, and a one-line reason. The five ticked rows sit above a thin green divider; the two crossed rows sit below it on a very pale grey ground. One strip of text runs along the bottom. Flat illustration, thin dark outlines, flat fills.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly 7 rows, each with 4 cells: the code, a thumbnail construction, a tick or a cross, and a one-line reason.
- Rows 1 to 5 are SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS, each with a green tick, above a thin green divider.
- Rows 6 and 7 are AAA and SSA, each with an orange cross, below the divider on a very pale grey ground.
- Thumbnails: SSS two circles crossing above and below a base; SAS two arms from a hinge with the angle marked between them; ASA a base with two rays crossing once above it; AAS a triangle with two angles given and the third filling in; RHS a right angle with an arc meeting above and below and a fold line; AAA three nested triangles with the same angles in three sizes; SSA a gate with two landings on the same side.
- The bottom strip holds one line about the middle letter.

Visible text:
- SSS
- SAS
- ASA
- AAS
- RHS
- AAA
- SSA
- Three sides. Nothing left free.
- The angle is between. Both arms pinned.
- Two rays cross exactly once.
- Get the third angle. Now it's ASA.
- The second landing is just a flip.
- Angles fix the shape, not the size.
- The gate can land in two places.
- Look at the middle letter.
- In SAS the angle is between.
- In ASA the side is between.
- In SSA the angle has slipped to the end.

Critical rejection conditions:
- a tick on AAA or SSA, or a cross on any of the five working rows
- a thumbnail construction that is inaccurate, such as the SAS angle drawn outside the two arms or the AAA triangles drawn at the same size
- orange or muted red anywhere outside the two crosses and the two failed rows
- any publisher, source or page mark anywhere in the frame
- fewer or more than seven rows
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a right angle drawn visibly different from 90 degrees, or a right-angle mark on a corner that is not a right angle
- tick marks that do not match the equal sides and angles stated, or a pair of figures that is not congruent when the picture says it is

Student takeaway: Five conditions work and two do not, and the middle letter tells you whether the angle is between the sides.

maths_rules: The wall chart has seven rows in this order: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS, AAA, SSA. Each row has a code, a small picture from its own topic, a mark and a one-line reason. The marks stay empty until the narration reaches the row.

The five rows that work (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS) get a green tick and sit above a thin green divider. The two that fail (AAA, SSA) get an orange cross and sit below it. The orange colour is used only for the two failed rows and for some students's wrong idea.

The picture for AAA is one triangle drawn at three sizes with the same angle arcs on all three; the three do not land on each other. The picture for SSA is the swinging gate landing in two places on the same line.

media.title: Right Angle Rescue
media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'The Repaired Case', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
The student comes back to the gate stage met before, with three changes. The base angle dial snaps to 90 degrees with a click and a small square appears at that corner. The line from that end of the base is drawn upward and downward, full length, in grey. A fold lever folds the stage along the base, so whatever is above swings down onto whatever is below. Dials set the base from 2 to 12 centimetres, the base angle from 10 to 170 degrees and the swinging side, the hypotenuse, from 1 to 14 centimetres. SWING drops landing dots, teal above the base and amber below it, and a compare panel holds the two built triangles with SAME and DIFFERENT buttons.

Before pressing SWING, the student predicts whether the second landing will be a new triangle or the first one flipped. Card 1 sets a right angle, base 4 and swinging side 5: one dot lands above and one below. Card 2 presses BUILD BOTH, which puts the two triangles side by side, and the student presses SAME or DIFFERENT. Card 3 asks for proof, by pulling the FOLD lever. The upper triangle swings down onto the lower one and the figure goes green: 'They landed on each other. One triangle, two ways up.' A student who chose SAME after a successful fold hears 'And you proved it with the fold, not by looking.'

Cards 4 and 5 take the right angle away. With the base angle at 30 degrees, base 6 and side 4, both dots land above the base. Building both and folding, the triangles do not land on each other and are outlined in orange: 'These really are two different triangles.' Card 6 puts the right angle back and tries a swinging side of 3.5 on a base of 4. 'It never reaches the line,' because the side opposite the right angle must be longer than the base. Card 7 asks for two landings on the same side of the base with a right angle. The student tries bases and sides, presses impossible, and picks the reason: with the right angle the arc always cuts once above and once below, never twice on one side.

Hints ask whether the two dots sit on the same side of the base or on opposite sides; then what the fold does to them; then whether the swinging side is longer than the base. In free play every dial is free, the angle can snap to 90 degrees or roam, and a map mode draws a coloured strip of which side lengths give no landing, one or two for a fixed base. Through doing, the student learns that a right angle at the end of the base makes the second landing a mirror image of the first, so two sides and a right angle give one triangle, which repairs the two-sides-and-any-angle trap.

content.text:
Remember the swinging side that could land twice? When it was shortened, the two landings slid together into one, and the corner there was a right angle. So what happens if we start with a right angle?
Draw a base QR of four centimetres. At Q, draw a straight line up at a right angle. Set the compass to five centimetres, put it at R and swing an arc. The arc cuts the upright line once, above Q. Call that point P and join it to R.
Now carry the upright line downwards, below the base. The same arc cuts it again, at a point P'. There are two landings, as there were before.
Fold the paper along QR. P comes straight down and lands exactly on P'. The second triangle is the first one flipped over, and a flip is allowed. There is only one triangle.
Compare it with the earlier case. There, both landings were on the same side of the base, and the two triangles were really different. Here the landings are on opposite sides, so they are mirror images.
The long side opposite the right angle is called the hypotenuse. A right angle, the hypotenuse and one more side fix the triangle. The short name for this is RHS, for right angle, hypotenuse, side.

content.text:
Two triangles each have a right angle, a base of 4 cm next to it and a long side of 5 cm opposite it. Are they congruent? Construct the triangle and find out whether different triangles can exist.
1. Draw the base QR of 4 cm.
2. At Q, draw a long straight line at a right angle to QR.
3. Set the compass to 5 cm, put it at R and swing an arc. It cuts the upright line at a point above Q.
4. Mark that point P and join P to R. Triangle PQR has a right angle at Q, QR = 4 cm and PR = 5 cm.
5. Anyone who follows these steps gets this triangle, and the upright side PQ comes out as 3 cm.
Answer: Yes. Every triangle built from a right angle, a 4 cm base and a 5 cm long side is the same triangle, so they are congruent.

content.text:
Carry the upright line downwards below the base. Would the arc cut it there too? Is the triangle below also congruent to triangle PQR?
1. Extend the upright line below QR. The same arc of 5 cm from R cuts it again, at a point P'.
2. That makes a second triangle P'QR, with the right angle at Q, QR = 4 cm and P'R = 5 cm.
3. Fold the paper along QR. P lands exactly on P', so triangle PQR lands on triangle P'QR.
4. The two landings are on opposite sides of the base, so the second triangle is the first one flipped, and a flip is allowed.
5. So there is only one triangle, and any two triangles with a right angle, a 4 cm side and a 5 cm long side are congruent. The long side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, and this condition is called RHS.
Answer: Yes. The arc cuts the line below as well, and triangle P'QR is triangle PQR flipped over QR, so the two are congruent.

content.text:
Everything from this topic goes onto one wall chart. The chart has seven rows, not five. Five rows are rules that work. Two rows look like rules but do not work, and they belong on the chart too, so the list does not look random.
Row one is SSS. Three sides leave nothing free, so one triangle is possible. Row two is SAS. The angle is between the two sides, so both arms are pinned. Row three is ASA. Two rays cross exactly once.
Row four is AAS. Find the third angle, and it becomes ASA. Row five is RHS. The right angle folds the second landing away. All five get a green tick.
Row six is AAA. Equal angles fix the shape but not the size, so a triangle can be zoomed bigger or smaller and keep every angle. Row seven is SSA. The free side can land in two places on the same line. Both get an orange cross.
There is one trick that saves a lot of trouble: look at the middle letter. In SAS the middle letter is the angle, so the angle is between the two sides. In ASA the middle letter is the side, so the side is between the two angles. In SSA the angle has slipped to the end, and that is exactly what is wrong with it.

content.text:
Name the conditions that are enough to guarantee two triangles are congruent, and name the two that look as if they should work but do not.
Answer: Five conditions work: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS. Two do not: AAA, because equal angles fix the shape and not the size, and SSA, because the free side can land in two places.

content.text:
- With a right angle at the end of the base, the swinging side lands once above the base and once below it, never twice on the same side.
- The two landings are mirror images across the base, so the two triangles land on each other when one is folded over. That is one triangle, two ways up.
- In a right triangle the side opposite the right angle is the longest, so it must be longer than the base or it never reaches the line.
- Two sides and a right angle that is not between them are enough: that is the repair for the two-sides-and-any-angle trap.
