media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the folded hook, on the folded triangle): The two bottom corners landed exactly on each other. What do you think that means about the two bottom angles? Answer: no right answer, this is a prediction. Also accept: equal, the same, they match, I do not know, anything at all. If stuck: Just say what the fold makes you think. If wrong (what the child says): none, a prediction cannot be wrong; if the child says equal, say that is exactly it, and in two minutes you will be able to say why, which is the harder half. Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip and the turn): The triangle is turned on its side. Are the two matching angles still the two at the bottom? Answer: no, they turned with the triangle, so where they sit on the paper is not the reason. Also accept: no, not at the bottom any more, they moved, they turned with it. If stuck: Look at the triangle resting on a different side. Where did the two matching angles go? If wrong (yes, they are at the bottom): Look again at the turned triangle. The matching angles went with it. What stayed the same about them? Position on the paper is never a reason. Stop 3 (after the two right angles): AB equals AC was given, and we drew the two right angles. Where is the third match? Answer: AD is in both triangles. Also accept: AD, the free side, the crease, the line down the middle, it is shared. If stuck: You have two separate triangles on screen. Which side did we have to draw twice? If wrong (BD equals DC): That is true, but we do not know it yet. We would have to prove it, and we are using this match to prove other things. Find something nobody has to tell us. Stop 4 (after the free side): A right angle, the longest side, and one more side. Which rule is that? Answer: RHS. Also accept: RHS, R H S, right angle hypotenuse side. If stuck: Which of the rules you know has a right angle in its name? If wrong (another rule): Look at the matched parts again. One is a right angle. Which rule starts with a right angle? Stop 5 (the your-turn question, at the end): A bus shelter has two equal poles that meet at the top at an angle of thirty-six degrees. What is each of the other two angles? Answer: seventy-two degrees each, because the three angles add to one hundred and eighty, so the other two share one hundred and forty-four and are equal. Also accept: 72, 72 degrees, seventy-two. If stuck: One hundred and eighty take away thirty-six. Share it between two equal angles. If wrong (one hundred and forty-four): Careful, one hundred and forty-four is what the two of them share. Now split it. Folded hook: Fold It Down the Middle, the paper triangle cut and folded, opens this video as its first beats, and its one prediction question, what the fold means about the two bottom angles, is the first stop. Watch for M8: a child who says that if two angles are equal the sides must be too has said something true and reasoned badly. Reply: that is true, but it is not what we just proved; it is the sentence the other way round, and those are two different claims. Good spot, we will come back to it. Watch for M7: a child who wants to measure angle B and angle C after the proof is reminded, warmly, what free from twins means. The book numbers are not reused: the video uses fifty, sixty-five, one hundred, forty, ninety, forty-five and thirty-six degrees.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after Chintu's slip): We have shown angle B equals angle C. Which pair of sides should I pick next, to get a different pair of angles? Answer: AB and BC. Also accept: AB and BC, two different ones, BC and AC, any other pair, the bottom one and a side. If stuck: Which pair have we not used yet? If wrong (AB and AC again): We have already used that pair, it only ever tells us about B and C. We need a pair that involves A. Stop 2 (after the three equal blocks): Three equal angles adding to 180. Each one is? Answer: 60 degrees. Also accept: 60, 60 degrees, sixty, 180 divided by 3. If stuck: Three the same, adding to 180. If wrong (180): That is what all three make together. Share it into three equal parts. Stop 3 (the your-turn question, at the end): In triangle PQR, PQ equals PR and the angle at P is 40 degrees. What is angle Q? Answer: 70 degrees, because angle Q equals angle R and the two share 180 take away 40, which is 140. Also accept: 70, 70 degrees, seventy. If stuck: 180 take away 40 is 140. Share it between two equal angles. If wrong (140): Careful, 140 is what the two of them share. Now split it. Watch for M7: a child who wants to measure the angles afterwards is reminded that the fact already gave the answer. Watch for M8: a child who says equal angles must mean equal sides has said something true but different. It is the sentence the other way round, so say it is a separate claim to test on its own. The sixty is held back until the second stop. The book asks the child to verify by construction, and the Fold the Isosceles tool does that, so this video does not.

media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'Equal Sides, Equal Angles', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
The student gets a teal triangle in the centre of a white stage with three draggable corner handles. A panel on the left always reads out the three side lengths and the three angles live. The student can tap any two sides to lock them equal, drag a dashed pink crease from any corner to the opposite side, press snap to altitude, and pull a fold lever to fold the triangle along the crease. A small angle tracker shows the two base angles side by side, with a green link between them whenever they are equal. Press measure and press impossible complete the controls.

The student predicts whether the two halves will land, then locks two sides equal, drags the crease from the corner where they meet, and pulls the lever. The folded half turns amber and settles on the other half. If they coincide the figure flashes green and the word LANDED appears. If not, the overhang is outlined in orange with its size shown: 'It hangs over. This one doesn't fold onto itself.' While the student drags a corner of the locked triangle, the tracker keeps the two base angles linked in green, with no words, and the student notices it unaided.

Card 1 locks two sides, snaps to altitude and folds. Card 2 hides the base angles and asks whether they are equal. Card 3 makes the equal sides 7 centimetres and the top angle 80 degrees; the student works out 50 degrees each, then presses measure, and from this card on the base angles stay hidden until then. Card 4 uses a triangle with no equal sides and folds from each of the three corners: it never lands. Card 5 locks all three sides equal, and it lands from all three corners. Card 6 reads off its angles, 60 degrees each. Card 7 reverses the question: the student drags a triangle until the tracker links two angles and then looks at the two sides opposite, which are equal as well. Card 8 asks for two equal sides with different opposite angles. The student presses impossible and picks the reason: the fold down the middle always lands and carries one angle exactly onto the other.

Hints ask what the fold does to the two bottom corners; then whether the halves land when two sides are equal and when none are; then which angles the crease carries onto each other. Free play adds a trace mode that keeps a faint outline of every triangle made, and a gallery of six to recreate by dragging: equilateral, right isosceles, 3-4-5, a very flat one, a very tall one, and one with angles of 30, 60 and 90 degrees. Through doing, the student learns that a triangle folds onto itself exactly when two sides are equal, that the fold is why the two angles opposite them are equal, and that two equal angles bringing two equal sides is a second fact, not the same sentence turned round.

content.text:
Cut an isosceles triangle out of paper, a triangle with two equal sides. Fold it from the top corner straight down, and bring the two bottom corners together. They land exactly on each other, not nearly but exactly.
A child who has done this has already seen the result. The rest of the work explains why it happens, using the twin test from this chapter.
Take triangle ABC with AB equal to AC and the angle at A equal to eighty degrees. Draw the line from A straight down to BC, at a right angle to it. Call the point where it meets BC point D. This line is called the altitude from A.
Pull the two triangles apart: triangle ADB and triangle ADC. AB equals AC, because that was given. The two angles at D are both ninety degrees, because we drew them that way. AD belongs to both triangles, so it equals itself, a free side.
A right angle, the longest side and one more side is the rule called RHS. So triangle ADB is congruent to triangle ADC.
Matching parts of twins are equal, so angle B equals angle C. Nobody measured either one. In a triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
Now the numbers. The three angles add to one hundred and eighty degrees, and the top angle is eighty. So the other two share one hundred degrees. They are equal, so each one is fifty degrees.
This result runs one way: equal sides give equal angles. The other way round, equal angles give equal sides, is a different sentence. It is also true, but it is not what was just shown, and it needs a proof of its own.

content.text:
An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. What about its angles? We will not measure a single one.
Pick two of the sides. AB and AC are equal, so the triangle is isosceles with those two, and the angles opposite them are equal: angle B equals angle C.
Now pick a different two. AB and BC are also equal, so it is isosceles again, the other way round. Angle A equals angle C. All three angles are equal.
Three equal angles add up to 180 degrees, so three times one angle is 180. Each angle is 60 degrees. One fact, used twice, and no protractor.

content.text:
In an equilateral triangle ABC all three sides are equal. What can we say about its angles?
1. AB = AC, so the triangle is isosceles with those two sides, and the angles opposite them are equal: angle B = angle C.
2. AB = BC as well, so the triangle is isosceles in a second way, and the angles opposite them are equal: angle A = angle C.
3. So angle A = angle B = angle C: all three angles are equal.
4. The three angles add up to 180 degrees, so 3 × angle = 180 and each angle is 180 / 3 = 60 degrees.
Answer: All three angles are equal, and each one is 60 degrees.

3. So angle A = angle B = angle C: all three angles are equal.
4. The three angles add up to 180 degrees, so 3 × angle = 180 and each angle is 180 / 3 = 60 degrees.
Answer: All three angles are equal, and each one is 60 degrees.

content.text:
Look for triangles in the five pictures: a glass pyramid, a stone pyramid, a dome, a rangoli star and a bridge. In each one the same triangle is repeated again and again, so the triangles are twins.
In the dome, a factory can make a thousand panels from one mould, so every panel is a twin of the next. In the rangoli, one triangle is turned by the same amount round the centre each time, so the copies are twins by turning.
A triangle is the only shape whose sides fix it completely. A square frame can be pushed over into a slanted diamond. A triangle frame cannot be pushed out of shape at all.
That is why bridges and domes are built from triangles. Three sides fix the shape, and that is why the Howrah Bridge is still standing.

content.text:
Describe the congruent triangles you see in each of the five pictures.
1. Louvre pyramid: the four sloping glass faces are congruent triangles, and each face is made of many small congruent triangular panes.
2. Pyramid of Giza: the four sloping faces are congruent triangles.
3. Dome: it is built from many congruent triangular panels, repeated all over its surface.
4. Rangoli: the star is made from one triangle repeated, and each copy is turned by the same amount about the centre, so the copies are congruent by turning.
5. Howrah Bridge: the truss is a line of congruent triangles, each identical to the next, and that is what gives the bridge its strength.
Answer: Each structure repeats one triangle: four faces on each pyramid, many panels on the dome, turned copies in the rangoli, and a line of identical triangles in the bridge truss.

maths_rules: Triangle AIR is congruent to triangle FLY: A matches F, I matches L, R matches Y; the sides AI and FL, IR and LY, RA and YF match; the angles at A and F, I and L, R and Y match.
Case 1: AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = DF, no angles; the rule is side side side and triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.

Case 2: AB = EF, angle A = angle E, AC = ED; the sketch shows AB and AC from A with the angle at A between them, and EF and ED from E with the angle at E between them; the rule is side angle side and triangle ABC is congruent to triangle EFD.

Case 3: AB = DF, angle B = angle D = 90 degrees, AC = FE; the right angles are at B and D, the hypotenuses are AC and FE, a leg is AB and DF; the rule is right angle hypotenuse side and triangle ABC is congruent to triangle FDE.
Case 4: angle A = angle D, angle B = angle E, AC = DF; two angles and a side that is not between them; the rule is angle angle side and triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.
Case 5: AB = DF, angle B = angle F, AC = DE; the sketch shows the angle at B is not between AB and AC; this is side side angle and it does not guarantee congruence.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): The first case has three equal sides and no angles. Which rule fits it? Answer: side side side, SSS. Also accept: SSS, side side side, the three sides one. If stuck: Count the sides and count the angles. If wrong (an angle rule): There is no angle in the list at all. Which rule uses only sides? Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Count the sides and the angles in the first case. Which rule uses only those? Answer: side side side, SSS. Also accept: SSS, side side side. If stuck: Three sides and no angles. Which of the rules uses only sides? If wrong (side angle side): That rule needs an angle, and this list has none. Count again. Stop 3 (after Chintu's slip): In the fifth case, is the angle at B between the sides A B and A C? Answer: no. Also accept: no, it is not, no it is at the end, side side angle, SSA. If stuck: Sketch it. Put your finger on A B and on A C. Is B squeezed between them? If wrong (yes): Draw it quickly. A B and A C both start at A, so the angle between them is at A, not at B. The right angle hypotenuse side case is taught on screen without a pause. Stop 4 (after case four is described): The fourth case has two equal angles and a side that is not between them. Which rule is that? Answer: angle angle side, AAS. Also accept: AAS, angle angle side, two angles and a side that is not between them. If stuck: Where does the side sit, between the two angles or outside them? If wrong (angle side angle): Angle side angle needs the side between the two angles. Is it between them here? Honesty note: case four, two angles and the side A C, is angle angle side; the third angle is then equal too, so it is angle side angle after one step. Watch for M9: a child who names a rule from the letters alone, without a sketch, is told to draw the two triangles first.

video_script.anchor: How can triangles show that two lines never meet?
video_script.design: One idea: twin triangles give a free angle, and an angle pair across a transversal decides whether two lines ever meet. It assumes the child knows SAS, matching parts of twins and the angles at a crossing. The wrong idea is some students's: any rule can be run backwards. The anchor question stays up all video; one clear at the part boundary before the recap.
source: Proving two lines never meet: the crossing question and its triangles
Using equal alternate angles to show two lines are parallel
never_show: the answer to the your-turn question: the strings never meet, because the triangles at the nail are twins
a verdict that a rule works backwards just because it works forwards
video_script.wrong_move: some students thinks any rule can be run backwards without checking; the rule a square has four equal sides run backwards fails, because a tilted diamond has four equal sides and is not a square.
maths_rules: The figure has A top left, C top right, B bottom left and D bottom right. The segments AD and BC cross at O. AB is the left side and CD is the right side. OA and OD carry one tick each, and OB and OC carry two ticks each. No length or angle is written anywhere.

The two triangles are AOB on the left and DOC on the right. The statement is triangle AOB congruent to triangle DOC, read A on D, O on O, B on C. The matches are OA = OD (given), OB = OC (given) and angle AOB = angle DOC (vertically opposite, the angle between the two sides), so the rule is SAS.

Angle OAB = angle ODC because they are matching parts of the twin triangles. AD is the transversal cutting AB and CD, and these two angles sit between the lines on opposite sides of it, so they are alternate angles. Equal alternate angles mean AB and CD are parallel.

The measured cases in the ground use two lines cut by one transversal. Case one has alternate angles of 50 degrees and 50 degrees and the lines never meet. Case two has 65 degrees and 65 degrees and the lines never meet. Case three has 50 degrees and 65 degrees and the lines lean together and meet if drawn long enough.

some students's claim, a rule that works one way works backwards too, fails on the rule a square has four equal sides: run backwards, a tilted diamond has four equal sides and is not a square. The diamond is drawn with four equal sides and visibly slanted corners, and no angle is written on it.

The reverse used in the proof is said out loud: parallel lines give equal alternate angles, and here equal alternate angles give parallel lines. The video says this rule happens to work both ways and does not prove the reverse; the ground cases are only the hint.

your turn: two strips PS and QR are nailed together at their middles at O, with P top left, Q top right, R bottom left and S bottom right. String joins P to R on the left and Q to S on the right. The answer, the strings never meet, is never shown.
video_script.payoff_line: Equal alternate angles mean the lines are parallel

final_answer.value: AB and CD are parallel: triangles AOB and DOC are twins by SAS, so angle OAB equals angle ODC, and these alternate angles are equal
final_answer.spoken: the two triangles are twins, so the alternate angles are equal, and the lines are parallel

video_script.substitution: Twin triangles at the crossing give a free pair of equal angles, and equal alternate angles across a transversal mean the lines are parallel.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the hook, on the figure): Nothing in the question mentions a triangle. Where could two triangles be hiding in this picture? Answer: one on the left, with corners eigh, O and B, and one on the right, with corners D, O and C, both meeting at the crossing O. Also accept: the two triangles at O, left and right, one each side of the cross, the two with eigh B and C D in them, I do not know. If stuck: Put a finger on O. Which two lines come out of it on the left, and what joins their ends? If wrong (the top and bottom ones): Those need extra lines to be drawn. Which triangles are already there, with all three sides drawn? Stop 2 (after Chintu's slip): Can we run a rule backwards without checking it? Answer: no, a rule run backwards is a different rule and needs its own reason. Also accept: no, not always, you have to check, it can be false, only if it is true. If stuck: Think of the tilted diamond. It has four equal sides. Is it a square? If wrong (yes, it works both ways): If that were so, the diamond would be a square. Look at its corners. A rule backwards must be checked each time. Stop 3 (after the two given matches): Two matches are given. Where does the third one come from? Answer: the angles at O, facing each other across the crossing, which are vertically opposite. Also accept: the angles at O, free angles, vertically opposite, where the lines cross, the opposite angles. If stuck: You have met this crossing before, in the topic on crossing sticks. What was free there? If wrong (eigh B equals C D): That is what we are trying to find out about, so we cannot use it yet. Look at the crossing point itself. Stop 4 (after the twins are written): The triangles are twins. So what do we now know about angle O eigh B and angle O D C? Answer: they are equal. Also accept: equal, the same, they match, free from twins. If stuck: Free from twins. What does that say about matching parts? If wrong (they add up to something): Matching parts of twin triangles are equal. Which parts are these two? Stop 5 (the your-turn question, at the end): Two strips are nailed together at their middles at O, and strings join the left ends and the right ends. Will the two strings ever meet? Answer: no, they never meet. The two triangles at the nail are twins by side angle side, because the strips are nailed at their middles and the angles at the nail are free angles. So the alternate angles at the ends of one strip are equal, and the strings are parallel. Also accept: they are parallel, the triangles are twins, equal alternate angles, no because the angles match. If stuck: Which two triangles meet at the nail? Are they twins? After the answer, ask why. If wrong (yes they meet): Find the two matching sides and the free angle at the nail first. Then ask what the twins give for free. Watch for M8: a child who objects that the rule is being run backwards has spotted what most students never notice. Congratulate them, and say that it is allowed here only because this rule happens to work both ways. The video does that out loud, and never hides it. The first stop is an addition to the Flow, which has no stop in its opening, and it is the topic seed for the hidden triangles (M6). The word parallel is used for lines that never meet. The railway picture comes before this video as a talk image.

maths_rules: Square ABCD has A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left, and the line AC cuts it into triangle ABC and triangle ADC.
AB = AD and CB = CD because the sides of a square are equal, and AC is common, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC by SSS.
Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA with A onto C, B onto D and C onto A: AB = CD, BC = DA and CA = AC, all equal, so both statements are correct.
Correct matchings: 1 for three different sides, 2 for two equal sides, 6 for three equal sides.
Circle: A is the centre, B and C lie on the circle, so AB = AC are radii, the triangle is isosceles, angle A = 120 degrees, angle B + angle C = 180 - 120 = 60, and each is 60 / 2 = 30 degrees.
The first triangle is teal and the second amber; only a landed match is green and some students's wrong idea uses the warning colour.
video_script.payoff_line: The more equal sides, the more ways to match

final_answer.value: Yes, ABC is congruent to ADC and to CDA; one way for three different sides, two ways for an isosceles triangle, six ways for an equilateral triangle; angle B = angle C = 30 degrees
final_answer.spoken: yes, both statements are correct; two ways for two equal sides, six ways for three equal sides; angle B and angle C are thirty degrees each

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (after the book question): Is triangle ABC also congruent to triangle CDA? Answer: yes. Also accept: yes, both are correct, it also lands, yes it matches in a second way. If stuck: Read the letters in order: A goes onto C, B onto D, C onto A. Do the three pairs of sides match? If wrong (no): Do not guess from the names. Match the letters in order and check each pair of sides, then say again. Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): Do all three pairs of sides match when A goes onto C, B onto D and C onto A? Answer: yes, AB = CD, BC = DA and CA = AC. Also accept: yes, they all match, all three are equal. If stuck: Start with AB and CD. They are both sides of the square. If wrong (no): Check one pair at a time. AB and CD are sides of the same square. Stop 3 (after Chintu's slip): Which tile drops into its hole in the most ways? Answer: the one with all three sides equal. Also accept: equilateral, the one with all sides equal, the one with three equal sides. If stuck: Which tile looks the same however you turn it? If wrong (the one with two equal sides): Close, that one gives two. Is there a tile that is even more symmetric? Stop 4 (the circle question): AB and AC are both radii of the circle. What kind of triangle is ABC? Answer: isosceles. Also accept: isosceles, two equal sides, it has two equal sides. If stuck: Both AB and AC go from the centre to the edge. What does that make them? If wrong (equilateral): Only two sides are known to be equal. What do you call a triangle with exactly two equal sides? Watch for M5: a child who writes the second statement without matching the letters in order is told to say it as an instruction, first letter onto first letter. The answers: the two statements are both correct, the counts are one, two and six, and angle B and angle C are thirty degrees each. The talk image is shown before this video and asks how many ways each tile drops in.

Check it, thirty-four and forty-four make seventy-eight, and one hundred and eighty take away seventy-eight is what? Stop 2 (the hint, before the second try): What is left of one hundred and eighty for the third angle? Answer: one hundred and two degrees. Also accept: 102, a hundred and two. If stuck: Add the two given angles first, then take that total away from one hundred and eighty. If wrong (seventy-eight): That is the two angles added. The third angle is what is left of one hundred and eighty. Stop 3 (after Chintu's slip): Is seventy-eight the third angle? Answer: no, it is the two known angles added together; the third angle is what is left of one hundred and eighty. Also accept: no, no it is not, that is only two of them, it is not enough. If stuck: All three angles must add to one hundred and eighty. Does seventy-eight reach it? If wrong (yes): Seventy-eight is thirty-four plus forty-four. That is only two angles, so the third is still to find. Stop 4 (after the one hundred and forty-six): A triangle has two equal ticked sides and thirty-four degrees between them. What is each of the two equal angles? Answer: seventy-three degrees each. Also accept: 73, 73 each, both 73. If stuck: Equal sides mean equal angles. One hundred and eighty take away thirty-four is one hundred and forty-six, shared between two. If wrong (one hundred and forty-six): That is the pair together. Now split it between the two of them. Honesty note: only three instances are verified, 180 - 34 - 44 = 102, (180 - 34) / 2 = 73 and the corner check 56 + 34 = 90. The remaining angles are left to the child, left to the child to work out one triangle at a time; check them against the printed book only in the tutor's own copy; never quote any other angle as if it were checked. Watch for M6: a child who freezes at the whole figure is told, do not look at the picture, look at one triangle, and cover the rest with a hand.

media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'Putting the Rules to Work', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
The student works at a board in three bands. The top band shows the problem's figure with its given facts printed beneath it in plain words, and tapping any side or angle pulls a fact block out of it. The middle band is the fact shelf, where grey blocks are what the question told and green blocks are free. Four free-fact badges sit beside it: free side, free angles, free from parallel and free from twins. The bottom band is the chain: three empty slots, an arrow, a rule slot, an arrow and a conclusion slot. A route counter sits at the top right.

The student predicts which three facts the figure will need, taps parts of the figure to collect them, drags a badge in when a fact comes free, puts three blocks in the slots, picks a rule from the menu (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS or none of these) and presses check. A holding chain makes the figure show the two triangles separate, land on each other and go green. An and so row then appears, where any further equal part can be claimed with the free from twins badge: 'Free from twins. You never measured it.' A rule that does not fit the blocks gets 'Look at your three blocks. How many are sides and how many are angles?' Two sides and an angle not between them make the figure swing the third side and show two possible triangles: 'That chain won't hold.'

The nine cards are: a rectangle cut by its diagonal BD, where AB = CD, AD = CB and the free side BD give SSS; the kite, where SSS and the twins show AC cuts angle BAD in half; the X figure, where AO = OD, BO = OC and the free angles at O give SAS and then AB = CD; the hourglass, where free from parallel twice and DC = AB give ASA; and two equal angle pairs with the free side BC, giving ASA and then angle BAC = angle BDC. Card 6 is an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC and a line AD to the base, to be shown with equal base angles in two routes: AD as the altitude with RHS, or as the angle bisector with SAS. Card 7 shows AB parallel to CD from SAS and the equal alternate angles of the twins. Card 8 is the square in two ways, SSS with two matchings. The counter reads routes found 1 of 2 on cards 6 and 8 and never reveals the second route; clear route or new route starts another and keeps the first. Card 9 gives two triangles sharing a side with one more equal pair, so the student presses not enough: two matches and no way to a third.

Hints ask how many of the three facts are sides and how many are angles; then to sketch and put a finger on the angle: is it between the two sides? In free play the student builds any two triangles, marks parts as equal, and the tool says whether it is enough and which rule it is. Through doing, the student learns that an argument is a chain from facts to a rule to twins to every matching part, and that knowing the facts are not enough is a real answer.

content.text:
A case list gives three facts about two triangles, and you have to say whether the triangles are twins. There is a method, and it has four steps.
Step one, count. How many of the three facts are sides, and how many are angles? Step two, sketch. Draw both triangles roughly and mark the three facts on them. The letters can mislead you. The picture does not.
Step three, place. Is the angle between the two sides? Is the side between the two angles? Step four, name the rule that fits, or say that no rule is guaranteed.
Sketching is the step most people skip, and it is the one that matters. A list like AB = EF, angle A = angle E, AC = ED looks like a jumble of letters. Once you draw it, it is plainly two sides with the angle between them.
Before the five cases there is a warm-up. When a statement says triangle AIR is congruent to triangle FLY, the order of the letters already tells you which corner lands on which.

content.text:
Two segments, AD and BC, cross at a point O. A joins to B on the left, and C joins to D on the right. OA equals OD and OB equals OC, and both facts are given. The question is strange: show that the lines AB and CD never meet, not even if they were drawn on for a kilometre.
Nothing in the question mentions triangles, yet the triangles do the work. Pull triangle AOB and triangle DOC apart. OA equals OD is given. OB equals OC is given.
The angles at O face each other across the crossing, so they are vertically opposite and equal. That is a free angle, equal without being told. Two sides and the angle between them match: side angle side. So triangle AOB is congruent to triangle DOC.
Twins give free matches. Angle OAB equals angle ODC, because they are matching parts of twins. Nobody measured either one.
Now look at where those two angles sit. The line AD runs across both AB and CD, and a line that crosses two others is called a transversal. The two equal angles lie on opposite sides of AD, one beside AB and one beside CD. Angles placed like that are called alternate angles.
Usually the rule is used one way: if the lines are parallel, the alternate angles are equal. Here it is used backwards: if the alternate angles are equal, the lines are parallel. A rule run backwards is a different rule, so say so aloud. This one happens to work both ways. So AB is parallel to CD.
The proof has three steps: the triangles are twins, the angles are equal for free, and equal alternate angles make the lines parallel.

content.text:
The number of correct matches depends on how symmetric the triangle is. A triangle with all three sides different matches its twin in one way.
A triangle with two equal sides matches in two ways, because the equal sides can be swapped. A triangle with all three sides equal matches in six ways.
The circle question is short and uses the last topic: two radii are equal, so the triangle is isosceles, and the other two angles share what the top angle leaves.

content.text:
A figure full of lines looks like one hard problem. It is not. It is many small problems, and each one is easy once you look at only one triangle.
Find a triangle with two angles already known. The third angle is one hundred and eighty degrees take away the other two.
Find a triangle with two sides marked the same. The two angles opposite those sides are equal.
Find a straight line or a corner. Angles on a straight line make one hundred and eighty degrees, a corner of the rectangle makes ninety degrees, and all the way round a point makes three hundred and sixty degrees.
Write each answer on the picture, then go round again. Every answer you write unlocks the next triangle.

content.text:
- An argument is a chain: facts lead to a rule, the rule leads to twin triangles, and twin triangles give every matching part for free.
- Three facts must be the right three: look at how many are sides, how many are angles, and where they sit.
- The four free facts are a side shared by two triangles, angles that face each other where two lines cross, alternate angles across parallel lines, and matching parts of twin triangles: nobody has to tell you them.
- Two sides and an angle that is not between them can land two ways, so that chain does not hold.
- Knowing that the facts are not enough is a real answer.

concepts.concept_name: Putting the Rules to Work: Ans2

steps: Case (a): count first. Three sides and no angles, so the rule is side side side. A goes with D, B with E and C with F, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.

Case (b): count first. Two sides and one angle. Sketch it: AB and AC both start at A, and the angle is at A, so it sits between them. In the other triangle, EF and ED both start at E, with the angle at E between them. The rule is side angle side, and the statement is triangle ABC congruent to triangle EFD.

Case (c): there is a right angle, so check the right angle, hypotenuse, side rule. The right angles are at B and D. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, so it is AC in one triangle and FE in the other, and they are equal. A leg is equal too, AB = DF. The statement is triangle ABC congruent to triangle FDE.

Case (d): two angles and a side, and the side AC is not between the two angles. The third angles are equal too, because the three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. The rule is angle angle side, and the statement is triangle ABC congruent to triangle DEF.

Case (e): two sides, AB and AC, and the angle at B. Sketch it and ask whether B is squeezed between AB and AC. It is not, because AB and AC both start at A. So the angle is not between the two sides, and no rule guarantees that the triangles are twins.
content.answer: (a) Congruent, side side side: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. (b) Congruent, side angle side: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle EFD. (c) Congruent, right angle hypotenuse side: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle FDE. (d) Congruent, angle angle side: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. (e) Not guaranteed: the given angle at B is not between AB and AC, so it is the side side angle arrangement.

$1$. Case $(a)$: count first. Three sides and no angles, so the rule is side side side. A goes with $D$, $B$ with $E$ and $C$ with $F$, so triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$.
$2$. Case $(b)$: count first. Two sides and one angle. Sketch it: $AB$ and $AC$ both start at $A$, and the angle is at $A$, so it sits between them. In the other triangle, $EF$ and $ED$ both start at $E$, with the angle at $E$ between them. The rule is side angle side, and the statement is triangle $ABC$ congruent to triangle $EFD$.
$3$. Case $(c)$: there is a right angle, so check the right angle, hypotenuse, side rule. The right angles are at $B$ and $D$. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, so it is $AC$ in one triangle and $FE$ in the other, and they are equal. A leg is equal too, $AB = DF$. The statement is triangle $ABC$ congruent to triangle $FDE$.
$4$. Case $(d)$: two angles and a side, and the side $AC$ is not between the two angles. The third angles are equal too, because the three angles of a triangle add up to $180$ degrees. The rule is angle angle side, and the statement is triangle $ABC$ congruent to triangle $DEF$.
$5$. Case $(e)$: two sides, $AB$ and $AC$, and the angle at $B$. Sketch it and ask whether $B$ is squeezed between $AB$ and $AC$. It is not, because $AB$ and $AC$ both start at $A$. So the angle is not between the two sides, and no rule guarantees that the triangles are twins.

concepts.concept_name: Putting the Rules to Work: Ans4

steps: AB = AD and CB = CD because the sides of a square are equal, and AC belongs to both triangles, so it is equal to itself.
Three sides match, so triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC.
Try A onto C, B onto D and C onto A: AB = CD, BC = DA and CA = AC all hold, so triangle ABC is also congruent to triangle CDA.
Any isosceles triangle matches its twin in two ways, because the two equal sides can be swapped over.
An equilateral triangle matches in six ways, because every pairing of the letters lands.

media.teaching_notes: Stop 1 (the closing question, at the end): Two triangles share one side. What do you know about that side, for free? Answer: a side shared by two triangles is equal to itself, a free fact. Also accept: it is equal to itself, it is the same in both, it is a free side, it is shared so it matches. If stuck: Pull the two triangles apart in your head. Which side did you have to draw twice? If wrong (it is longer or shorter): The same line sits in both triangles. Can it be a different length in each? This is a recap, so nothing new is taught and the rest of the video plays straight through. The wall chart picture (image 10) is shown by reference alongside this video.

media.title: Six Congruent Pieces
media.context: Class 7 'Geometric Twins'. The one tool of the topic 'What the Twins Taught Us', on its practice concept after the teaching. The child works it alone; the tutor hands it over in one line and asks one question afterwards. It applies the idea and never replaces the teaching. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not built.
media.description:
A five by five grid sits in the centre of the stage, with the middle square solid green and out of play and the other 24 squares white with thin borders. Six colours are ready, one for each piece. On the right, a panel holds small thumbnails of the pieces built so far, and two pieces that are twins, turns and flips allowed, are joined by a green line. Two plain counters are always visible, squares used and pieces made, for example squares used: 20 of 24 and pieces: 5. A control bar has next piece, undo, clear all and check all, and each thumbnail has rotate and flip buttons.

Card 1 comes before any painting: how many squares are in play, and how many must each piece have? The student works out 24 squares shared by six pieces, so 4 each, which settles the size before the shape. Card 2 asks for one piece of four squares of any shape. The student taps squares to paint them into the current piece, taps a painted square again to remove it, and presses next piece to close it. Card 3 asks for a second piece congruent to the first. The student can rotate or flip a thumbnail by hand and watch it land on the other, and when the two are twins the panel draws a green link with no words. Pieces that are not twins have no link, so the student learns to trust the link and the landing test, not the eye.

Card 4 asks for all six. The counters rise as squares are painted, and check all lights only when all 24 squares are used and there are exactly six pieces. Then each piece lifts, turns and lands on the first, as a tracing would: 'Six pieces. Every one a twin.' The full solution is six L-shaped pieces, some of them turned or flipped. Card 5 asks for the 24 squares in 5 congruent pieces. After trying, the student presses impossible and picks the reason: 24 does not divide by 5, so the pieces could not all be the same size.

Hints ask how many squares each piece must have before any shape is tried; then whether a turned or flipped piece is still a twin, with the thumbnail lifted and turned by hand; then what the panel's link says about two pieces. In free play the grid resizes to 4 by 4, 5 by 5 or 6 by 6, the blocked square can be moved or removed, and the student sets how many pieces to make. Some settings have no solution and the tool does not say which. Through doing, the student learns that congruent is a demand you can build to and not only a question you answer, that size comes first and shape second, and that if the squares cannot be shared out evenly then equal pieces are impossible whatever the shape.

content.text: You have met a lot of rules in this chapter. If you could keep only one habit for a hard picture, what would it be?

content.text:
The chapter began with a sign painter and a notebook. Two figures are congruent, twins, when one lands exactly on the other. You may turn a figure and flip it while you check, so a twin can lie any way up.
You never have to check everything. Every shape has a short list of measurements that leaves no choice. A circle needs one number, a rectangle needs two, and the signboard symbol needs three.
For triangles, five lists work. Side side side: three sides. Side angle side: two sides and the angle between them. Angle side angle: two angles and the side between them. Angle angle side: two angles and a side that is not between them. Right angle, hypotenuse, side: a right angle, the hypotenuse and one more side.
Two lists look as if they should work and do not. Angle angle angle fixes the shape and says nothing about the size, like a photo zoomed in. Side side angle, with the angle not between the sides, leaves a loose side that can land in two places.
A congruence statement is an instruction: put the first corner on the first corner, the second on the second, the third on the third. If you shuffle the letters on one side, shuffle the other side the same way.
Four facts come free. A side shared by both triangles is equal to itself. Opposite angles at a crossing are equal. Alternate angles across parallel lines are equal. And once two triangles are twins, every matching part is equal.
Congruence then does the proving. Fold an isosceles triangle down the middle and the halves are twins, so the two base angles are equal. Use that twice on an equilateral triangle and every angle is sixty degrees.
If you keep one thing, keep this. When a picture looks impossible, pull the two triangles apart, mark what you know on both, and count to three.

If you keep one thing, keep this. When a picture looks impossible, pull the two triangles apart, mark what you know on both, and count to three.

content.text:
What are the main ideas of the chapter, in order?
Answer: Congruent figures land exactly on each other, and turning or flipping is allowed. Triangles are congruent by side side side, side angle side, angle side angle, angle angle side or right angle, hypotenuse, side. Angle angle angle and side side angle do not guarantee it. Matching parts of congruent triangles are equal. Angles opposite equal sides are equal, and each angle of an equilateral triangle is sixty degrees.

content.text:
Draw lines to split the 24 white squares of the five by five grid, with the middle square left out, into 6 smaller regions that are all congruent.
1. Count what is in play first: 25 squares less the blocked middle one leaves 24.
2. Six congruent pieces must be the same size, so each gets 24 / 6 = 4 squares.
3. Turning and flipping a piece is allowed, so each piece can lie any way up.
4. Lay a tracing of one piece over each other piece, turning or flipping it, to confirm that all six land.
Answer: Six pieces of four squares each. Size first: 24 / 6 = 4 squares in every piece. Other layouts may also work.

tool_three_sticks.title: Three Sticks
tool_three_sticks.predict: Three sticks have a hinge at every joint. Before you build, can the same three sticks make two triangles that are not twins?
tool_three_sticks.one_idea: Once the three stick lengths are fixed, the triangle is fixed too, and the only freedom left is which way up it lies.
tool_three_sticks.invariant: Three fixed side lengths leave no freedom in a closed triangle, so every build is the first one slid, turned or flipped; and a triangle closes only when two sides together are longer than the third.

tool_twin_checker.title: Twin Checker
tool_twin_checker.predict: Two figures look alike. Before you move the tracing, will it land exactly, or will something stick out?
tool_twin_checker.one_idea: Two figures are congruent exactly when one can be made to land on the other by sliding, turning and flipping, and nothing else.
tool_twin_checker.invariant: Sliding, turning and flipping never change a length or an angle, so a pair that differs in size can never land.

tool_proof_builder.title: Proof Builder
tool_proof_builder.predict: A figure has two triangles hidden in it and a few facts given. Before you build the chain, which three facts do you think it will need?
tool_proof_builder.one_idea: An argument is a chain: facts lead to a rule, the rule leads to twins, and twins give you everything else for free. You can see the whole chain at once if you lay it out instead of writing it in a paragraph.
tool_proof_builder.invariant: A chain holds only when the three blocks in the slots fit the rule chosen; every part claimed afterwards comes from the twins and was never measured.

tool_shortest_list.title: Shortest List
tool_shortest_list.predict: Before you press send it, will four painters draw the same figure from your list, or will they differ?
tool_shortest_list.one_idea: A list of measurements is long enough exactly when nobody can draw a second, different figure that obeys it.
tool_shortest_list.invariant: A list is long enough only if every figure that obeys it is the same figure; angles alone leave the size free, so they never force it.

tool_swinging_gate.title: Swinging Gate
tool_swinging_gate.predict: The gate is a side that can swing. Before you pull SWING, how many places do you think it can land on the ray: none, one or two?
tool_swinging_gate.one_idea: When the angle is between the two sides, the triangle is forced. When it is not, the loose side is a gate that can land in two places, and the number of landings depends on how long the gate is.
tool_swinging_gate.invariant: The tip of the gate stays the gate length away from Q, so it can land only where that distance meets the ray; with the angle between the two sides, that leaves exactly one place.

tool_name_the_twins.title: Name the Twins
tool_name_the_twins.predict: You write the statement, and the triangle obeys it letter by letter. Before you press the button, will your statement land exactly, or will a corner hang over?
tool_name_the_twins.one_idea: The congruence statement is an instruction. Whatever you write, the triangle will obey it literally, so a wrong statement produces a visibly wrong landing.
tool_name_the_twins.invariant: Slot 1 lands on slot 4, slot 2 on slot 5 and slot 3 on slot 6, so a statement is correct exactly when each pair of matched corners has equal sides around it.

tool_pull_them_apart.title: Pull Them Apart
tool_pull_them_apart.predict: A kite has a line drawn from its top corner to its bottom corner. Before you pull anything out, how many matches do you think the two triangles will give you?
tool_pull_them_apart.one_idea: Any tangled geometry picture becomes an easy one the moment the two triangles are physically separated and marked up.
tool_pull_them_apart.invariant: Pulling a triangle out of a figure changes no length and no angle, and a side shared by both triangles is equal to itself, so the free match is always there.

tool_angle_side_angle.title: Angle Side Angle
tool_angle_side_angle.predict: Two rays leave the two ends of a base, each at an angle you set. Before you press COUNT CROSSINGS, will they cross once, twice, or sometimes not at all?
tool_angle_side_angle.one_idea: Two angles at the ends of a known side send out two rays, and two rays cross in exactly one place, so there is exactly one triangle.
tool_angle_side_angle.invariant: Two rays from the ends of a base that are not parallel meet in exactly one point, so the base and the two end angles fix one triangle; if the end angles add to 180 degrees or more they never meet.

tool_fold_the_isosceles.title: Fold the Isosceles
tool_fold_the_isosceles.predict: A triangle has two equal sides. Before you fold it down the middle, will the two halves land exactly on each other?
tool_fold_the_isosceles.one_idea: A triangle folds onto itself exactly when two of its sides are equal, and the fold is why the two angles opposite them must match.
tool_fold_the_isosceles.invariant: Folding along the line from the top corner to the middle of the base lands exactly when two sides are equal, and then it carries one base angle onto the other, so the two angles stay equal however the triangle is reshaped.

tool_right_angle_rescue.title: Right Angle Rescue
tool_right_angle_rescue.predict: Put a right angle at the end of the base and swing the side. Before you press SWING, will the second landing be a new triangle, or the first one flipped?
tool_right_angle_rescue.one_idea: With a right angle at the base, the arc's second landing is always on the other side of the base, so it is a flip and not a new triangle.
tool_right_angle_rescue.invariant: With a right angle at the end of the base, the two landings sit on opposite sides of the base at equal distances, so they are mirror images and give one triangle; the side opposite the right angle must be longer than the base to reach the line.

tool_six_congruent_pieces.title: Six Congruent Pieces
tool_six_congruent_pieces.predict: Six pieces must all be twins of one another. Before you paint, how many squares will each piece have?
tool_six_congruent_pieces.one_idea: Congruent is a demand you can build to, not just a question you answer, and the first thing to work out is not the shape of the pieces but their size.
tool_six_congruent_pieces.invariant: Pieces that are twins have the same number of squares, so the squares in play must share out evenly among the pieces before any shape is tried.

source_metadata.chapter_idea: Two figures are twins when one can be laid exactly on the other, turning and flipping allowed. You never have to check everything: a short list of matching measurements is enough. Knowing which short lists work, and which ones only look as if they should, is the whole chapter. Once two triangles are twins, every matching part is equal, for free.

objectives.objective_text: Decide which measurements of a symbol leave no choice, by testing two lengths and then adding the angle between them, and write the fewest numbers that make every copy identical.
Decide whether two figures are congruent by tracing one and dropping the tracing on the other, and explain that size means every length and every angle, not only the area.
Decide whether a figure that has been slid, turned or flipped is still a twin of the original, and name the move that brings a mirror-image pair to land.
Decide whether two figures are congruent by sliding, turning and flipping a tracing until it lands or cannot, and give a reason when no amount of moving will make it land.
List the fewest measurements that pin down a circle, a rectangle and the signboard symbol, and decide whether two figures are congruent by comparing those measurements.
List the measurements that pin down a figure of three arms meeting at a point, by counting what could still change, and explain why the third angle needs no measuring.
Decide how few measurements of a circle, a rectangle, a square, a three-armed figure and a triangle leave no second figure possible, and explain why angles alone can never fix the size.
State which side you take, Meera's three sides or Rabia's angles, and say why a smaller copy of the frame lets you test it by drawing.
Draw a triangle from sides of four, six and eight centimetres using two circles, explain why the two crossing points give twin triangles, and state the condition for two triangles to be congruent.
State the SSS condition in your own words, and decide whether two triangles are twins by finding a partner for each side, even when the lengths are listed in a different order.

Decide whether three straight rods can close into a triangle, and test by flipping and turning whether any two triangles built from the same three lengths are different, giving a reason when it cannot be done.
Decide which corner of one triangle lands on which corner of its twin by matching the sides first, list the three pairs of corners, and say why the matching angles are equal without measuring them.

Write the congruence statement for two twin triangles from the list of corners that land on each other, and decide whether a re-ordered statement keeps the same matching by shuffling both sides alike.

Name the side that two triangles in one picture share, explain why it is equal to itself, and write the correct matching of corners and the congruence statement for the two triangles a rectangle's diagonal makes.

Write the congruence statement for two triangles as a record of which corner lands on which, list all six correct ways of writing it, and explain why a statement with the corners in the wrong order fails.
Find the two triangles hidden in a tangled figure, redraw them apart, mark the equal parts on both, and count the matches, then write the congruence statement with the corners in the right order.
Fill in a two-column sheet for a figure, writing what the question tells in one column and what can be taken for free in the other, and list the four free facts before choosing a rule.

Separate the two triangles hiding in a tangled figure, mark the equal sides and angles on both, count the matches, name the rule that applies and write the congruence statement with the corners in the right order.
Decide whether two triangles with the same three angles must be congruent, by drawing them at different sizes, and explain why angles fix the shape but not the size.
Construct a triangle from two sides and the angle between them, measure the closing side, decide whether every classmate gets the same triangle, and say where the angle sits in the letters S, A, S.
Decide whether two sides and an angle that is not between them fix a triangle, by constructing it and counting the places the loose side can land, and explain why one triangle is not guaranteed.
Count how many triangles a base, an angle and a loose side can make, find the lengths of loose side that give none, one or two, and explain why an angle between the two sides gives exactly one.
Construct a triangle from a base and the two angles at its ends, decide whether every classmate gets the same triangle, and say which letter sits in the middle of A, S, A and why.
Find the missing third match in a figure of two crossing lines by marking the angles that face each other as equal, and decide that two outer sides are equal because their triangles are twins.

Find the missing third angle of a triangle by subtraction from 180 degrees, decide whether two triangles are congruent when the side is not between the given angles, and name the rule that fits each picture.
Build a triangle from a base and the two angles at its ends, count where the two rays cross, and explain why they cross in one place only, so the triangle is forced.
Decide whether a right angle, the longest side and one more side fix a triangle, by swinging the arc above and below the base, and explain why the second landing is only a flip.
List the five conditions that guarantee two triangles are congruent, name the two that fail and say why, and use the middle letter of a code to tell where the given angle sits.
Test a right angle at the end of the base, count where the swinging side lands above and below the base, and explain why the second landing is the first one flipped, so one triangle only.
Explain why the two angles opposite the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are equal, by splitting it along a line from the top corner, and find both base angles when the top angle is given.
Explain why every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees, by using the equal-angles fact for two different pairs of equal sides, and then find each angle by dividing the angle sum by three.

Describe where congruent triangles appear in five real structures, decide how the repeated triangles are copies of one another, and explain why a triangle frame holds its shape when a square frame does not.
Test which triangles fold onto themselves, by locking sides equal and folding along a crease from a corner, and explain why two equal sides always bring the two opposite angles together.
Sort three given facts about two triangles by counting the sides and angles and checking where the angle sits, then name the matching rule or decide that no rule is guaranteed.
Prove that two lines are parallel by finding twin triangles, taking a pair of equal angles from them, and showing those angles are alternate angles on a line that crosses both lines.
Count the correct ways to match a triangle onto its twin by looking at how many sides are equal, and use two equal radii to find the base angles of a triangle drawn inside a circle.
Find the missing angles in a crowded figure by picking one triangle, straight line or corner at a time, writing each answer on the figure, and going round again until no angle is left blank.
Build a chain from three facts to a rule to twin triangles, then claim a further equal part, find two routes where they exist, and decide when the facts given are not enough.
List the five rules that make two triangles congruent and the two that fail, and state the three moves for a picture that looks impossible: pull the triangles apart, mark the given parts, count.
Work out how many squares each piece needs before painting, then split twenty-four squares into pieces that are all twins of one another, and explain why five equal pieces cannot be made.
